﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾: an address to all people in general. We have already discussed taqwa (God-consciousness) at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

﴿from a single soul﴾: this is Adam, peace be upon him.

﴿and its mate﴾: this is Eve, who was created from Adam's rib.

﴿and spread﴾: i.e., dispersed.

﴿by whom you ask one another﴾: meaning, some of you say to others, "I ask you by Allah to do such-and-such."

﴿and the wombs﴾ with the accusative (بالنصب): it is in coordination with the name of Allah, meaning: fear the wombs (i.e., the ties of kinship), so do not sever them. Or it is in coordination with the place of the prepositional phrase, "وهو به" (and He is with it), because its place is accusative. It was also read in the genitive (بالخفض), coordinated with the pronoun in "به" (by it). This is weak according to the Basran grammarians (al-Basriyyun), because a pronoun in the genitive cannot be coordinated with unless the preposition is repeated.

﴿Indeed, Allah has ever been Watchful over you﴾: when the servant truly realizes this verse and similar ones, he attains the station of muraqabah (constant awareness of Allah's watchfulness), which is a noble station. Its root is knowledge and state, and then it yields two states. As for knowledge, it is the servant's awareness that Allah is informed about him, observes him, sees all his deeds, hears all his words, and knows everything that crosses his mind. As for the state, it is the constant presence of this knowledge in the heart, to the extent that it dominates him and he does not neglect it. Knowledge alone is not sufficient without this state. When knowledge and state are attained, their fruit for the People of the Right (أصحاب اليمين) is haya' (modesty) before Allah, which necessarily requires abandoning sins and striving diligently in acts of obedience. Their fruit for those brought near (المقربين) is witnessing, which necessitates reverence and veneration of the Possessor of Majesty.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) alluded to these two fruits when he said: "Ihsan (excellence) is that you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you." His saying "that you worship Allah as if you see Him" points to the second fruit, which is witnessing that necessitates reverence, like one who beholds a great king and thereby necessarily venerates him. His saying "if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you" points to the first fruit. Its meaning: if you are not among those who witness, which is the station of those brought near, then know that He sees you, so be among those of haya', which is the station of the People of the Right. When he first explained ihsan by the highest station, he saw that many people may be unable to reach it, so he descended to the other station.

Know also that muraqabah is not sound unless it is preceded by mushara†ah (stipulation) and murabata (covenant), and followed by muhasaba (self-accounting) and mu'aqaba (chastisement). As for mushara†ah, it is the servant's stipulation upon himself to commit to obedience and abandon sins. As for murabata, it is the servant's pledge to his Lord regarding that. Then, after mushara†ah and murabata at the outset, muraqabah continues to the end. After that, the servant calls himself to account for what he stipulated and pledged. If he finds himself having fulfilled what he pledged to Allah, he praises Allah. If he finds himself having dissolved the stipulation and broken the covenant, he punishes the self with a chastisement that restrains it from returning to the like. Then he returns to mushara†ah and murabata, maintains muraqabah, and is tested by muhasaba. Thus it continues until he meets Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 2:

﴿And give the orphans their property﴾. This is addressed to the guardians (al-awsiya'). It was also said: it is addressed to the Arabs who did not give inheritance to the young along with the old; they were commanded to give them their inheritance. On the view that the address is to the guardians, the meaning is that they should give the orphans from their property what they eat and wear in their childhood; thus "orphan" here is literal (haqiqah). It was also said: the meaning is handing their property over to them when they reach maturity; thus "orphan" here is figurative (majaz), because the orphan has grown up.

﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾. Some of them would replace a fat sheep from the orphan's property with a lean one from their own, and a good dirham with a counterfeit one, so they were forbidden from this. It was also said: the meaning is, do not consume their property, which is the bad, and leave your own, which is the good.

﴿And do not consume their property along with your property﴾. The meaning: he forbade them to consume the orphans' property by combining it with their own property. It was also said: he forbade mixing their property with the orphans' property. Then he permitted that by His saying: ﴿And if you mix with them, then they are your brothers﴾. The verb was made transitive with "ila" (to) only because it implies the meaning of gathering and combining. It was also said: "ila" here means "ma'a" (with).

﴿Hubaan﴾, i.e., a sin (dhanban).

﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphan girls, then marry﴾ ... the verse. ʿĀʾisha said: It was revealed concerning the guardians of orphans who were attracted to the beauty and wealth of their wards, and wished to marry them while cheating them on the bridal gift (ṣadāq) because of their authority over them. So it was said to them: Be just in their bridal gifts. Whoever fears that he will not act justly, then let him marry what is good for him of other women, who will be given their rights.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: The Arabs were scrupulous regarding the wealth of orphans, but were not scrupulous regarding justice among wives, so the verse was revealed about that; meaning, just as you fear that you will not act justly regarding orphans, so too fear regarding women. It was also said: a man among them would marry ten or more, and when his wealth ran short he would take the property of an orphan. So it was said to them: If you fear that you will not act justly regarding orphans, then limit yourselves regarding women to what is good (ṭāba): i.e., what is lawful (ḥalla).

He said "mā" and not "man" because he intended the category (jins). Al-Zamakhsharī said: because female rational beings are treated as non-rational beings, and from this is His saying ﴿what your right hands possess﴾ ﴿two, three, or four﴾. It is not declined (lā yanṣarif) due to being a fixed form (ʿadl) and a descriptive (waṣf), and it is a circumstantial (ḥāl) clause relative to "mā ṭāba."

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it is a substitute (badal). Its deviation from repeated numerals, and the sense of repetition in them, is that the address is to a group, so each one of them may marry whatever number he wishes from those numbers; thus the numbers are repeated with the repetition of people. The meaning is: marry two, or three, or four. In this there is a prohibition of what used to occur in the Jāhiliyya of marrying more than four.

Some people, whose view is not regarded, said: it is permissible to combine nine, because "two, three, and four" gives a total of nine. This is an error, because the intended meaning is choice among these numbers, not combination. Had He intended combination, He would have said "nine," and He would not have turned away from that to something longer and less clear. Furthermore, consensus (ijmāʿ) has been established on the prohibition of exceeding the fourth wife.

﴿So one﴾: i.e., if you fear that you will not be just between two, three, or four, then limit yourselves to one, or to what your right hands possess, whether few or many, out of desire for justice. The accusative of "wāḥida" is by a hidden verb whose estimate is: so marry one.

﴿That is closer to avoiding injustice (taʿūlū)﴾: The reference is to limiting oneself to one wife; the meaning is that this is nearer to your not being unjust. The meaning of taʿūlū is "to incline (tamīlū)." It was also said: "that your dependents become numerous."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 4:

﴿And give the women their dowers﴾. It is addressed to the husbands. It is also said that it is addressed to the guardians (awliya'), because some of them used to consume the dower of their ward. It is also said that it is a prohibition of *shighar* (a marriage in which two men exchange their unmarried daughters or sisters without a dower). ﴿*Nihlah*﴾ means a gift from you to them, or a gift from God. It is also said that the meaning of *nihlah* is *shir'ah* and *diyanah* (a sacred law and religion). Its being in the accusative is either as a verbal noun (*masdar*) from the sense of *ātūhunna*, or as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from the pronoun of the addressees. ﴿But if they give you willingly﴾ the verse: it is a permission for the husbands and the guardians, according to the disagreement mentioned earlier, to take what they gave the women of their dowers, with good pleasure of their souls. The pronoun in *minhu* refers to the dower or to the giving. ﴿Wholesome and agreeable﴾ is an expression of permissibility and an emphasis on the permission. They are two adjectives from your saying *hanu'a al-ta'am* and *mari'a*, when the food is palatable and free of any disturbance. They are descriptions of the verbal noun: i.e., eat wholesomely and agreeably, or they are a circumstantial accusative from the subject pronoun. It is also said that one pauses at *fakuluhu* and begins ﴿wholesome and agreeable﴾ as a supplication.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 5:

﴿And do not give the foolish your property, which Allah has made for you a means of sustenance⦆ It is said: they are the children of a man and his wife; that is, do not give them your property to squander. It is also said: "the foolish" are those placed under guardianship (al-mahjurun), and "your property" means the property of those placed under guardianship; it is attributed to the addressees because they supervise it and it is under their control. ﴿Qiyaman﴾ is the plural of qima (value), and it is also said to mean qiyaman (a means of support) with an alif, that is, your livelihoods are sustained by it. ﴿And provide for them from it and clothe them﴾: it is said this refers to those whose maintenance a man is obliged to provide, namely his wife and children; and it is also said it refers to those placed under guardianship, who are to be provided for and clothed from their own property. ﴿And speak to them a kind word﴾: that is, pray for good for them, or promise them a fair promise, meaning: if you wish, we will hand over your property to you.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashīl) on Sūrah al-Nisā', verse 6:**

﴿وَٱبْتَلُواْ ٱلْيَتَٰمَىٰ﴾ That is, test them: ﴿وَٱبْتَلُواْ ٱلْيَتَٰمَىٰ﴾ means ﴿test the orphans﴾ to see their *rushd* (sound judgment). ﴿بَلَغُواْ النِّكَاحَ﴾ means they have reached the age of the men, that is, the age of marriage. ﴿فَإِنْ آنَسْتُمْ مِّنْهُمْ رُشْداً﴾ *Rushd* is knowledge of how to look after their interests and manage their property, even if they are not among the people of religion. Some scholars made religiosity a condition. Mālik required both puberty and *rushd*, and only then is the property handed over. Abū Ḥanīfa required only puberty, provided no foolishness (*safah*) appears, but his view contradicts the Qur'an.

﴿وَبِدَاراً أَن يَكْبَرُواْ﴾ Its meaning is "hastening before they grow up," that is, the guardian seizes the opportunity to consume the orphan's property before he comes of age. The phrase ﴿أَن يَكْبَرُواْ﴾ is in the accusative, either as the object (*mafʿūl*, the direct object) of *bidāran* or as the object of purpose (*mafʿūl lahu*, the object showing the reason for the action). Its sense is: "for fear that they grow up."

﴿فَلْيَسْتَعْفِفْ﴾ The wealthy guardian is commanded to abstain (*yastaʿfif*) from the orphan's property and not to eat anything from it.

﴿وَمَن كَانَ فَقِيراً فَلْيَأْكُلْ بِٱلْمَعْرُوفِ﴾ ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said: the meaning is that a poor guardian may borrow from the orphan's property, and when he becomes well-off he repays it. It was also said: what is meant is that he may take a wage equal to his work and service. The meaning of *bil-maʿrūf* is "without extravagance." It was also said that this ruling was abrogated (*nasakhat-hā*, i.e., naskh, abrogation).

﴿إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ يَأْكُلُونَ أَمْوَٰلَ ٱلْيَتَٰمَىٰ ظُلْماً﴾ [al-Nisā': 10]

﴿فَأَشْهِدُواْ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ This is a command to take precaution and safeguard (*al-taḥarruz wal-ḥirz*), so it is a recommendation (*nadb*). It was also said that it is an obligation (*farḍ*).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 7:

﴿For men there is a share﴾ (the verse): its occasion of revelation was that some of the Arabs would not give inheritance to women, so the verse was revealed that men and women should both inherit. ﴿A share ordained﴾ is in the accusative (manṣūb) in the manner of an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkad) to his saying: "an obligation from Allah." Al-Zamakhshari said: it is in the accusative by way of specification (takhsīs), meaning: "as a share."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verses 8–10:

﴿And when the relatives and the orphans and the needy are present at the division (of the inheritance)﴾ etc.: This is an address to the heirs. They were commanded to give charity from the inheritance to their relatives, to the orphans and to the needy. It has been said that this is obligatory (wujub); it has been said that it is recommended (nadb), and this is the sound view; and it has been said that it was abrogated (naskh) by the verse of inheritance (ayat al-mawarith). ﴿And let those fear (Allah) who, were they to leave behind weak offspring, would be anxious for them﴾ etc.: Its meaning is a command to the guardians of orphans to treat them well in safeguarding their property, so that they fear Allah concerning their orphans just as they would fear for their own offspring if they left them weak, and that they imagine this within themselves so that they do not act contrary to compassion and mercy. It has also been said that it refers to those who sit beside a sick person and urge him to give away his wealth in charity until it harms his heirs; so they were commanded to fear for the heirs just as they would fear for their own children. The object of "wal-yakhsha" is omitted, and "khafu" is the answer (jawab) of "law" (if). ﴿And speak to them a fitting word﴾: According to the first view, it means the guardian's gentle speech to the orphan with good words; according to the second view, it means that he should say to the testator: "Do not be extravagant in your bequest, and be gentle with your heirs." ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾: It has been said that it was revealed concerning those who did not give inheritance to females; and it has been said that it was revealed concerning the guardians; but its wording is general, covering everyone who consumes an orphan's property without right. ﴿They are only consuming fire into their bellies﴾: That is, their consumption of orphans' property leads to their entry into the Fire. It has also been said that they consume fire in Hell.

This verse was revealed concerning the daughters of Sa'd ibn al-Rabi'. It is also said to have been revealed concerning Jabir ibn Abdullah, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) visited him during his illness. It abolished what was practiced in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period) of giving inheritance to women and children. It is also said that the bequest to parents and relatives was abrogated (naskh). The phrase ﴿يُوصِيكُمُ﴾ is in the present-tense verb form. Had he said ﴿أوصاكم﴾ (past tense), it would have been a reminder of what had passed and an introduction to a new ruling. He said ﴿يُوصِيكُمُ ٱللَّهُ﴾ with the explicit divine name rather than the pronoun, because he intended to magnify the bequest, so he used the name that is greatest among names. He said ﴿فِيۤ أَوْلٰدِكُمْ﴾ ("concerning your children") and not "concerning your sons" (abna'), because the word ibn applies to a foster son, to a daughter's son, and to a deceased son's son, and these are not all heirs. ﴿لِلذَّكَرِ مِثْلُ حَظِّ ٱلأُنْثَيَيْنِ﴾ ("for the male, the equivalent of the share of two females") is an explanation of the bequest mentioned. If it is asked: why not say "for the two females, the equivalent of the share of a male"? The answer is that the male is mentioned first.

﴿فَإِن كُنَّ نِسَآءً﴾ ("if they are women"): he made the plural pronoun in ﴿كُنَّ﴾ feminine because he intended the females. Its original reference is to the children, since that term includes males and females. It is also said that it refers to what was left behind. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that ﴿كان﴾ be a complete verb (kana tammah, meaning "to exist"), with the pronoun being unspecified and ﴿نِسَآءً﴾ as its explanation.

﴿فَوْقَ ٱثْنَتَيْنِ﴾ ("more than two"): its apparent meaning is more than two. For this reason there is consensus that for three or more females, the two-thirds share applies. As for two daughters, scholars disagreed. Ibn Abbas said they receive a half, like a single daughter. The majority said they receive two-thirds, by the Sunnah (prophetic tradition) and not by the Qur'an. It is also said that this is by analogy (qiyas) to the two sisters.

﴿وَإِن كَانَتْ وَٰحِدَةً﴾ ("if she is one"): with the nominative reading (raf') it is the subject of a complete ﴿كان﴾; with the accusative reading (nasb) it is the predicate of ﴿كان﴾. His saying ﴿فَلَهَا ٱلنِّصْفُ﴾ ("then for her is half") is an explicit text that a daughter receives half when she is alone. It is also evidence that a son receives the whole estate when he is alone, because ﴿لِلذَّكَرِ مِثْلُ حَظِّ ٱلأُنْثَيَيْنِ﴾ (the male receives the equivalent of two females' shares).

﴿إِن كَانَ لَهُ وَلَدٌ﴾ ("if he has children"): the word walad applies to male and female, singular, dual and plural alike, whether from the loins or a son's child. All of them return the parents to a sixth.

﴿وَوَرِثَهُ أَبَوَاهُ فَلأُمِّهِ ٱلثُّلُثُ﴾ ("and his parents inherit from him, then for his mother is a third"): God did not assign the mother a third except under two conditions: one, the absence of children; the other, that the two parents alone inherit. For this reason the conjunction "wa" (and) was used, to join one condition to the other. He remained silent about the father's share, relying on what is implied, since after the third only two-thirds remains, and there is no heir except the two parents. This requires that the father takes the remainder of the estate, which is two-thirds.

﴿فَإِن كَانَ لَهُ إِخْوَةٌ فَلأُمِّهِ ٱلسُّدُسُ﴾ ("if he has siblings, then for his mother is a sixth"): the scholars agreed that three siblings reduce the mother to a sixth. They disagreed about two. The majority held that two siblings also reduce her to a sixth. Ibn Abbas held that two siblings do not reduce her to it, but are like a single sibling. His argument is that the word ikhwah (siblings) does not apply to two, since it is a plural and not a dual, and the least plural is three. Others said that the plural form may apply to two, as in His saying: ﴿وَكُنَّا لِحُكْمِهِمْ شَٰهِدِينَ﴾ ("and We were witnesses to their judgment") and ﴿وَتَسَوَّرُوا ٱلْمِحْرَابَ﴾ ("and they climbed over the prayer niche") and ﴿وَأَطْرَافَ ٱلنَّهَارِ﴾ ("and the ends of the day"). They cited his (ﷺ) saying: "Two and what is above them is a congregation." Malik said: "The Sunnah has established that siblings are two or more," and his position is that the least plural is two. On this basis, the two parents are reduced from a third to a sixth, whether the siblings are full siblings, paternal, or maternal, or of mixed kinds, and whether they are male or female, or a combination. If a father is present with them, he inherits the remainder of the estate. The siblings receive nothing according to the majority, since they exclude the mother (hajb, exclusion) and do not inherit themselves. Some people said they take the sixth from which they excluded the mother. If there is no father, they inherit.

﴿مِن بَعْدِ وَصِيَّةٍ يُوصِي بِهَآ أَوْ دَيْنٍ﴾ ("after any bequest he makes or debt"): the phrase "min ba'di" (after) is connected to the implied stability in His saying "then for them are two-thirds of what was left," meaning: the two-thirds became theirs after a bequest. It is impossible for it to be connected to "taraka" (left), and the subject of "yusi" (bequeaths) is the deceased. The bequest was placed before the debt, although the debt takes precedence over it in the law, for the sake of giving it importance, emphasizing the command to it, and so that it would not be neglected. The debt was placed later because its owner demands it, so there is no need to stress the command to pay it. The bequest is paid from the third, and the debt is paid from the principal after the shroud. He mentioned "bequest" and "debt" in indefinite form, to show that they may exist and may not exist. This indicates that the bequest is obligatory.

﴿أَقْرَبُ لَكُمْ نَفْعاً﴾ ("closer to you in benefit"): it is said that this refers to spending on them when they are in need. It is also said that it refers to intercession in the Hereafter. It is possible that he means benefit through the inheritance from his wealth, and this is more fitting to the context of the discourse.

﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave﴾, the verse. This is addressed to men. The scholars reached consensus (ijma', agreement of the scholars) on what this verse contains regarding the inheritance of the husband and the wife. The wife's share is taken by her alone if she is one wife, and it is divided among them if there are more than one. It is not reduced below the shares of the husband, the wife, and the other fixed shares, except for what is reduced by 'awl (the increase in the total of the fixed shares, which requires proportional reduction) according to the view of the majority of scholars. Ibn 'Abbas differs, for he does not hold the view of 'awl.

If it is asked: why did He repeat ﴿after a bequest﴾ with the inheritance of the husband and the inheritance of the wife, when He mentioned it before only once, in the inheritance of the children and the parents? The answer is that the thing inherited in the husband's share is the wife, and the thing inherited in the wife's share is the husband. Each is a separate matter on its own, so it was mentioned with each one, unlike the first case, where the thing inherited is one. In it He mentioned the ruling on what his children and parents inherit from him, and it is one matter, so He said in it ﴿after a bequest﴾ only once.

﴿And if a man leaves property to be inherited as kalalah (a person who leaves neither children nor parents)﴾. Kalalah is the cutting off of the line of descent, that is, the deceased having no child and no father. It may be applied here to the deceased who is inherited from, or to the heirs, or to the relatives, or to the property. 

If it refers to the deceased, then its i'rab (grammatical parsing) is that it is the predicate of kana (كان, "was"), and yurathu (يورث, "is inherited") is in the position of a qualifier, or yurathu is the predicate of kana, and kalalah is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun in yurathu. Or kana is complete (تامة), and yurathu is in the position of a qualifier, and kalalah is a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun. If it refers to the heirs, it is a verbal noun (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial accusative. If it refers to the relatives, it is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih). If it refers to the property, it is the object of yurathu. Each of these aspects holds when kana is complete and yurathu is in the position of a qualifier, and also when kana is incomplete and yurathu is its predicate.

﴿and he has a brother or a sister﴾. The intended meaning here is a brother from the mother and a sister from the mother, by consensus. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas recited: ﴿and he has a brother or a sister from his mother﴾, and that is an explanation of the meaning.

﴿then for each one of them is a sixth﴾. If there is one brother from the mother, he has a sixth. Likewise, if there is one sister from the mother, she has a sixth. If the brothers from the mother are two or more, they are partners in the third, and they share it equally between male and female, because the word "partners" requires equality among them. There is no disagreement on this.

﴿without causing harm﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal). The element governing it is yusi (يوصي, "bequeaths"), and mudarr is an active participle. Ibn 'Abbas said: causing harm in a bequest is one of the major sins. The forms of harm are many. Among them: a bequest to an heir, a bequest exceeding one third, or a bequest of one third made to avoid giving a needy heir his share. If it is known that the one bequeathing intended harm by his bequest, the excess over one third is rejected by agreement. There is disagreement whether it is reduced to one third, and there are two opinions in the school. The well-known view is that it is executed.

﴿a bequest from Allah﴾ is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing His statement "Allah enjoins you" (يوصيكم الله). It is permissible for it to be in the accusative without being a verbal noun.

﴿Those are the limits of Allah﴾: a reference to what was mentioned earlier concerning the inheritance and other matters. ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ (the verse): the Mu'tazilah (a theological school that holds that the Muslim who commits major sins will abide forever in the Fire) cited it in support of their view that disobedient believers will abide forever in the Fire. The Ash'ariyyah (followers of the theological school of al-Ash'ari) interpreted it as referring to disbelievers. ﴿Commit a flagrant immorality﴾: here this means fornication (zina). ﴿From your women﴾, or from Muslim women, because a Muslim woman is subject to the prescribed punishment (hadd) for fornication. As for a disbelieving man or woman, scholars differed on whether they receive the hadd or a discretionary punishment (ta'zir). ﴿Then call four witnesses against them from among you﴾: it was said that four witnesses were required for fornication as a severity toward the accuser and a concealment of the people's faults. It was also said that it was so that there would be two witnesses for each of the two fornicators. ﴿Then confine them to their houses﴾: the punishment for fornication was confinement in the houses, and then this was abrogated (naskh) by the harm mentioned after it, which is reviling and rebuke. It was also said that confinement applies to women and harm applies to men, so there is no abrogation between them. Ibn 'Atiyyah (Ibn 'Atiyyah al-Andalusi) preferred this view, saying: confinement is for your women, and harm is from you. Then confinement and harm were abrogated by stoning for the married (muhsan) and by flogging for the unmarried. The matter became settled on this. As for flogging, it is mentioned in Surah al-Nur. As for stoning, it was in the Qur'an, then its wording was abrogated while its ruling remained. The Prophet (ﷺ) stoned Ma'iz al-Aslami and others. ﴿Then turn away from them﴾: when he commanded harming the fornicator, he commanded turning away from him once he repents, which means ceasing to harm him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (*al-Tashil*) on surah 4, verse 17:

﴿Repentance from Allah is only for those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon.﴾ Meaning: Allah only accepts the repentance of those who have this description. When a servant repents with a sound repentance that meets its conditions, then, according to the majority of scholars, Allah's acceptance of his repentance is certain. Abu al-Ma'ali said: this is a strong probability (*yaghlib 'ala al-zann*), but it is not certain.

﴿They do evil in ignorance﴾: that is, in foolishness and with little consideration of the act as a means to disobedience. The meaning is not that they hold the act to be disobedience. Abu al-'Aliyah said: the Companions (*al-sahabah*) agreed that every act of disobedience is done in ignorance, whether it was committed deliberately or out of unawareness.

﴿Then they repent soon﴾: it was said, before illness and death. It was also said, before the death rattle (*al-siyaq*) and before seeing the angels. On this, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah accepts the repentance of a servant as long as he has not yet begun the death rattle."

﴿And repentance is not [accepted]﴾ – the verse: It concerns those who persist in sins until the time when repentance is no longer accepted, which is the moment of witnessing death. If they were disbelievers, they will abide forever in the Fire by consensus (ijma'). If they were Muslims, they are subject to Allah's will: if He wills, He punishes them, and if He wills, He forgives them. So His words, ﴿We have prepared for them a painful punishment﴾, apply to the disbelievers and are abrogated (naskh) with respect to the sinful Muslims, by His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with; but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. Thus their punishment is restricted by His will.

**(Ibn Juzayy, *al-Tashil*, on Surah an-Nisa', verse 19)**

﴿It is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: In the Jahiliyyah, when a man died, his male relatives (awliya') had more right to his wife. If they wished, one of them would marry her; if they wished, they would marry her to someone else; and if they wished, they would prevent her from remarrying. So the verse was revealed concerning this. The meaning of the verse, according to this view, is: It is not lawful for you to treat women as an inheritance from men, as property is inherited. It was also said that the address is to husbands who keep a woman in the marriage bond ('ismah) in order to inherit her property without any real affection for her. It was also said that the address is to the guardians who prevent their female wards from remarrying, so that they may inherit them rather than the husband.

﴿And do not hinder them﴾: this is conjoined with "that you inherit," or it is a prohibition. *al-'adl* means preventing. Ibn 'Abbas said: This also refers to the relatives of the husband who prevent his widow from remarrying after his death, except that His words, ﴿what you have given them﴾, on this reading mean what the deceased man had given her.

Ibn 'Abbas also said: It refers to husbands who keep a wife and treat her badly until she ransoms herself with her dowry. This is the apparent sense of the wording in His words, ﴿what you have given them﴾, and it is strengthened by His words, ﴿and live with them honourably﴾. The more apparent reading is that it concerns husbands, though it may also apply to others. It was also said that it concerns the guardians.

﴿Unless they commit a flagrant immorality﴾: it was said that the "flagrant immorality" here is adultery. It was also said that it is the wife's disobedience (nushuz) and her hatred for her husband. If she is disobedient, it is permissible for him to take back what he gave her as dowry or anything else from her property. This is permissible according to the school of Malik regarding khul' (divorce initiated by the wife through compensation), when the harm comes from the wife. Adultery is more grievous to the husband than disobedience, so it is permissible for him to take the ransom (fidyah).

﴿And if you dislike them﴾, the verse means: if you dislike women for some reason, then be patient with it, for perhaps Allah will place good in another aspect. It was also said that the good is abundant offspring. The best view is that it is general, and this is the meaning of the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Let no believing man hate a believing woman; if he dislikes one trait in her, he will be pleased with another."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 20:

﴿And if you desire to replace one spouse with another﴾ etc. Its meaning is the prohibition of a man taking ransom (fidyah) from a woman in exchange for divorce if he wishes to replace her with another. On this basis the school of Malik and others went in prohibiting ransom when harm comes from the husband and the wife seeks separation. Some said that this verse has been abrogated (mansukh) by His saying in al-Baqarah: ﴿There is no blame upon them for what she gives up therefrom﴾ [Verse: 229]. Others said that it is the abrogating verse (nasikh). The sound view is that it is neither abrogating nor abrogated, for permitting ransom in one form and prohibiting it in another form means there is no contradiction and no abrogation. ﴿Qintar﴾ is an example given for the sake of emphasizing abundance. A woman used it as evidence for the permissibility of excessive dowry when ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab forbade that, and ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "A woman was right and a man was wrong; every person has more understanding than you, O ʿUmar."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 21:

﴿وَقَدْ أَفْضَىٰ بَعْضُكُمْ إِلَىٰ بَعْضٍ﴾ is a metaphor (kinaya) for sexual intercourse (al-jima'). ﴿وَأَخَذْنَ مِنكُم مِّيثَاقاً غَلِيظاً﴾ — it has been said: the "solemn covenant" is the bond of marriage (ʿuqdat al-nikah). It has also been said: it is His saying, ﴿فَإِمْسَاكٌ بِمَعْرُوفٍ أَوْ تَسْرِيحٌ بِإِحْسَانٍ﴾ [al-Baqara: 229] ("then either to retain with fairness or to release with kindness"). And it has been said: it is the command to treat (wives) well in companionship (husn al-ʿishra).

**Translation**

﴿And do not marry those women whom your fathers married﴾. Some of the Arabs used to marry the wife of their father after his death, so this verse was revealed to forbid that. Therefore, every woman a man has married becomes forbidden to his descendants, however far down the line, whether or not he consummated the marriage. The word *nikah* (marriage contract) in the verse means the contract ('aqd). *Ma nakaha* means the women, and the word *ma* was used for them because the intended meaning is the category (*jins*) of women.

If a man commits zina (unlawful intercourse) with a woman, scholars differ on whether marrying her becomes forbidden to his descendants. Abu Hanifa held that it is forbidden, while al-Shafi'i permitted it, and there are two opinions in the Shafi'i school. Those who prohibited it argued from this verse, understanding *nikah* in it to mean intercourse (*wat'*). Those who permitted it said that the verse does not cover this case, since *nikah* in it means the contract.

﴿except what has already passed﴾, meaning except what you did of that in the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance), which ended with Islam. It has been pardoned, so you will not be held accountable for it. This is shown by His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa': 23], after His saying ﴿except what has already passed﴾, in the case of the other woman: combining two sisters in marriage.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The Arabs used to forbid everything that the Shari'ah forbids, except the wife of the father and the combining of two sisters. It was also said that the meaning of ﴿except what has already passed﴾ is: marry them if it is possible for you, though that is not possible. So the meaning is an emphasis on the prohibition.

﴿Indeed, it was an abomination and hatred﴾. The word *kāna* (was) in this verse implies permanence, like His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa': 23], and similar phrases. Al-Mubarrad said that *kāna* is superfluous (*za'ida*), but this is an error, because its predicate appears in the accusative as *fāḥishatan wa maqtan* (an abomination and hatred). The verse adds this *maqt* (hatred) to what was described of zina in His saying, ﴿Indeed, it was an abomination and hatred, and evil was the way﴾. This indicates that this act is more hideous than zina.

﴿Forbidden to you are...﴾ the verse. Its meaning is the prohibition of the women mentioned. Women are forbidden permanently in three categories: by blood kinship (nasab), by fosterage (rida'), and by marriage affinity (musaharah). As for kinship, seven categories are forbidden by it. They are those mentioned in this verse. The rule governing them is that a man is forbidden his descendants (furu') however far down, his ascendants (usul) however far up, the descendants of his two parents however far down, and the first descendant of every ascendant is included alongside his parents. ﴿Your mothers﴾ includes the birth mother and the grandmothers, on the mother's side and the father's side, however far up they go. ﴿And your daughters﴾ includes the daughter, the son's daughter, and the daughter's daughter, however far down they go. ﴿And your sisters﴾ includes the full sister, or the sister by the father, or the sister by the mother. ﴿And your paternal aunts﴾ includes the father's sister and the grandfather's sister, however far up, whether full, paternal, or maternal. ﴿And your maternal aunts﴾ includes the mother's sister and the grandfather's sister, however far up, whether full, paternal, or maternal. ﴿And the daughters of the brother﴾ includes everyone descended from the full brother, or the paternal or maternal brother. ﴿And the daughters of the sister﴾ includes everything descended from the full sister, or the paternal or maternal sister.

﴿And your mothers who have nursed you, and your sisters through nursing﴾: God, exalted is He, mentioned two categories through nursing, namely the mother and the sister. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "What is forbidden through nursing is what is forbidden through lineage." This necessitates the prohibition of the seven categories that are forbidden through lineage, namely the mother, the daughter, the sister, the paternal aunt, the maternal aunt, the brother's daughter, and the sister's daughter. A detailed account of this would be lengthy. There are matters concerning nursing that we have not mentioned, because they have no connection to the wording of the verse.

﴿And the mothers of your wives﴾: those forbidden by marriage affinity are four. They are the father's wife, the son's wife, the wife's mother, and the wife's daughter. As for the first three, they are forbidden by the marriage contract, whether or not he has consummated the marriage with her. As for the wife's daughter, she is not forbidden except after consummation with her mother. If he has had intercourse with her, then her daughter is forbidden to him by consensus (ijma', the scholarly agreement). If he has enjoyed her by means short of intercourse, Malik and the majority have made her daughter forbidden to him. If he has contracted marriage with her and not consummated it, her daughter is not forbidden by consensus. These four are forbidden through nursing just as they are forbidden through lineage.

﴿And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, born of your wives﴾: the rabibah (stepdaughter) is the daughter of a man's wife by another man. She was so named because he raises her (yurabbihā), and so the word rabibah is of the form fa'ilah in the sense of maf'ulah (the one who is raised). His saying ﴿who are in your guardianship﴾ is according to what usually happens, since the stepdaughter is most often in the care of her mother's husband. She is forbidden whether she is in his guardianship or not. This is the position of the majority of scholars, except what is related from Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), that he permitted marrying her if she was not in his guardianship.

﴿With whom you have consummated marriage﴾: consummation was made a condition for the prohibition of the wife's daughter, and it was not made a condition for others. The majority of scholars hold this, except what is related from Ali ibn Abi Talib, that he made consummation a condition for the prohibition of all of them. Consensus was later established thereafter.

﴿And the wives of your sons﴾: the ḥalā'il (wives) is the plural of ḥalīlah, which means wife. ﴿Who are from your loins﴾ is a specification to exclude the wife of an adopted son, whom a man adopts while he is a stranger to him. Such is the marriage of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to Zaynab bint Jahsh, the wife of Zayd ibn Harithah al-Kalbi, who was called Zayd ibn Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿And that you combine two sisters﴾: this requires the prohibition of combining two sisters, whether they are full sisters or sisters by the father or by the mother, in the case of two wives. As for combining two sisters who are both slave-women in sexual intercourse, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa, and others prohibited it, and they held that it falls within the general wording "two sisters." The Zahiriyya permitted it, because they restricted the verse to combining through a marriage contract. As for combining two sisters in ownership without intercourse, it is permitted by agreement.

﴿Except what has already passed﴾: the meaning is: except what you did of that in the time of ignorance (jahiliyyah), which was ended by Islam. He has pardoned you for it, so you will not be held accountable for it. This is the most preferred of the opinions, as has been mentioned in the earlier passage.

﴿And the married women among the women﴾: here this means those who have husbands. It is joined to the prohibited categories mentioned before it. The meaning is that it is not permitted to marry a woman while she is under a man's marital bond (ʿişma).

﴿except what your right hands possess﴾: according to the most common opinion, this means captives (sabaya, sing. sabiyya). The exception is continuous (istithna' muttasil). The meaning is that if a disbelieving woman has a husband and is then taken captive, it is permitted for a Muslim who owns her to have intercourse with her. The reason is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent an army to Awtas, and they took captives from the enemy who had husbands among the polytheists. The Muslims felt sinful about having intercourse with them, so the verse was revealed permitting it. The school of Malik holds that capture destroys the marriage, whether both disbelieving spouses are taken together or one is taken before the other. Ibn al-Mawwaz said: capture does not destroy the marriage.

﴿the decree of Allah upon you﴾: this is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq, masdariyya). The meaning is: Allah has decreed a decree upon you, namely the prohibition of what has been prohibited. According to the Kufans, it is in the accusative as an incitement (al-ighra', a form of exhortation to take heed).

﴿and lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾: the meaning is that marrying women other than those who have been prohibited is lawful for you. "Lawful" (uhilla) is conjoined to the implied verb that governs "the decree of Allah," and the subject is Allah. That is, Allah has decreed upon you the prohibition of those mentioned, and has made lawful for you what is beyond that.

﴿that you seek [them]﴾: this is either an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi) or a substitute for "what is beyond that." Its object, which is "women," is omitted.

﴿chaste, [not] debauched﴾: here "chaste" (muhsinin) means modest and restrained (al-'iffa). It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject of "seek."

﴿not fornicators﴾: that is, not adulterers. Sifah (fornication) means zina.

﴿So whomever you have enjoyed of them, give them their wages as an obligation﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas and others said: its meaning is that if you have enjoyed a wife and intercourse has taken place, it becomes obligatory to give her the wage, which is the full dowry. It has also been said that it refers to temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'a), which is marriage for a fixed term without inheritance. It was permitted at the beginning of Islam, so this verse was revealed concerning the obligation of the dowry in it. Then it was prohibited according to the majority of scholars. On this view, the verse is abrogated (mansukh) by the established report prohibiting temporary marriage. It has also been said that it was abrogated by the verse of the inheritance shares, because there is no inheritance in temporary marriage. It has also been said that it was abrogated by ﴿and those who guard their private parts﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 5]. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he permitted temporary marriage, and it is narrated that he retracted it.

﴿And there is no blame upon you in what you mutually agree upon﴾: whoever says that the preceding verse concerns the dowries of women, then the meaning of this one is the permissibility of what they mutually agree upon, such as the wife reducing the dowry or deferring it after the obligation has been established. Whoever says that the verse concerns temporary marriage, then the meaning is the permissibility of what they mutually agree upon, such as an increase in the term of the temporary marriage and an increase in the wage.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 25:

﴿And whoever among you cannot afford the means to marry free, believing women﴾. Its meaning permits marrying slave girls, who are female slaves, to a man who cannot afford the means (ṭawl) to marry free women. Here ṭawl means wealth and ability. The word "muḥṣanāt" here means free women, not those owned as slaves.

The school of Mālik and most of his companions hold that a free man may not marry a slave woman except under two conditions. The first is the lack of ṭawl, meaning he cannot find the means to marry a free woman. The second is fear of ʿanat (the risk of falling into unlawful intercourse, zinā), based on His words after this: ﴿That is for whoever among you fears ʿanat﴾. Ibn al-Qāsim permitted marrying them without the two conditions, on the view that dalīl al-khiṭāb (argument from implication, that a stated condition implies its opposite) is not considered valid. They agreed that the slave woman being married must be a Muslim, based on the words of God Most High: ﴿from your believing slave girls﴾, except the people of Iraq, who did not require this.

On the grammatical analysis (iʿrāb) of ṭawlan: it is the object of "istiṭāʿa" (to be able). "An yankiḥa" is a substitute for it, and it is in the accusative position by implied "li-an yankiḥa." It is also possible that ṭawlan is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), with "istiṭāʿa" as its governing verb, since it means something close to "yatakārab" (to be able). On this reading, "an yankiḥa" is the object of "istiṭāʿa" or of the verbal noun.

﴿And God knows best your faith﴾: its meaning is that He knows the hidden matters and you know only their outward appearance. So if the slave woman's faith is apparent, her marriage is valid, and knowledge of her inner state rests with God.

﴿You are one from another﴾: that is, your slave women are from you, and this encourages marrying slave women, because some Arabs disdained this.

﴿So marry them with the permission of their people﴾: that is, with the permission of their masters who own them.

﴿And give them their wages﴾: that is, their dowries. This implies that they have more right to their dowries than their masters, and this is the view of Mālik.

﴿In a fair manner﴾: that is, according to the law as the Sunnah requires.

﴿Chaste, not fornicators﴾: that is, modest, not adulteresses. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and what governs it is "fankiḥūhunna" (so marry them).

﴿Nor taking lovers﴾: "akhdān" is the plural of "khadan," meaning a close companion. Among the women of the pre-Islamic age were some who took a lover with whom they committed adultery exclusively, and some who would not refuse anyone who touched them.

﴿And when they are chaste, if they commit a grave immorality, then for them is half the punishment of the free women﴾: the meaning is that if a slave woman commits adultery after she has been married (aḥṣanat), she receives half the prescribed punishment (ḥadd) of a free woman. A free woman is flogged one hundred lashes for adultery, and a slave woman is flogged fifty. Here "uḥṣina" means "tazawwajna" (married). "Al-fāḥisha" here means adultery, "al-muḥṣanāt" here means free women, and "al-ʿadhāb" here means the ḥadd. The verse thus establishes the ḥadd of a slave woman who commits adultery after marriage. The ḥadd of an unmarried slave woman is derived from the Sunnah, and it is like the ḥadd of the married one. This reading is with "uḥṣinna" with the hamza vowelled and the ṣād kasra; it was also read with both vowelled as fatḥa, and its meaning then is "they embraced Islam." It is also said that it means "they married."

﴿That is for whoever among you fears ʿanat﴾: the reference is to marrying a slave woman. That is, it is permitted only for one who fears for himself unlawful intercourse, not for one who controls himself.

﴿But that you be patient is better for you﴾: the intended meaning is patience in refraining from marrying slave women. This encourages leaving it, and its reason is what leads to the enslavement of the child.

Allah desires to make clear to you (﴿يُرِيدُ ٱللَّهُ لِيُبَيِّنَ لَكُمْ﴾). Al-Zamakhshari said: The original is "Allah desires that He make clear to you," and the lam was added to emphasize the desire for making clear, just as it is added in "la abaka" (by your father, no) to emphasize the attribution of the father. The Kufans said the lam is a verbal particle (lam masdariyya) like "an" (that). ﴿وَيَهْدِيَكُمْ سُنَنَ ٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ﴾ (and to guide you to the ways of those before you): that is, to guide you to the paths of those who came before you, of the prophets and the righteous, so that you may follow them. ﴿وَٱللَّهُ يُرِيدُ أَن يَتُوبَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ (and Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness): this is repeated as a preface against the corruption of the desire of those who follow their appetites. These, here, are the fornicators according to Mujahid. It was said: the Magians, because of their marriage to close relatives. It was also said: it is general to every one who follows a desire, and this is the more preferred view. ﴿يُرِيدُ ٱللَّهُ لِيُذْهِبَ عَنكُـمُ﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33]: the context of the discussion calls for the lightening that occurred in the permission to marry slave-women, and it is nevertheless general to everything by which Allah has lightened His servants' burden and made His religion easy.

﴿And man was created weak﴾. It was said: its meaning is that he cannot endure (patiently) [being apart from] women, and this is what the context of the discourse requires, but the wording is more general than that. ﴿Do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾ includes gambling, usurpation, theft, and other such things. ﴿Except that it be a trade﴾ is a disjunctive exception (istithna munqati', an exception whose excluded item is not part of the original group), and the meaning is: "But if it is a trade, then consume it." In the permissibility of trade there is evidence that a person may buy a commodity worth one hundred for one dirham, and the well-known position is that the sale is upheld. It is related from Ibn Wahb that it may be rescinded if the deception (ghabn) exceeds one third. The word أن (an) is in the accusative case, and تجارة (tijara) is in the nominative as the subject of تكون (takuna), where the verb is complete (tamma, meaning it needs only a subject). It is also read in the accusative as the predicate of تكون, where the verb is incomplete (naqisa, meaning it needs a predicate). ﴿From mutual consent among you﴾, meaning agreement. The Malikiyya (the Maliki school) used this as evidence that a sale is completed by the contract alone, without separation (of the parties), whereas al-Shafi'i said: it is only completed by separation of the bodies, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The two parties to a sale have the option (of cancelling) as long as they have not separated."

﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the scholars of tafsir unanimously agreed that the meaning is: none of you should kill another. I say: its wording also encompasses a person killing himself, and 'Amr ibn al-'As interpreted it in that sense, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not deny it when he heard him (say so).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verses 30–31:

﴿And whoever does that﴾: a reference to killing, since it is the nearest thing mentioned. It was also said that it refers both to that and to consuming wealth wrongfully, and it was also said that it refers to all the prohibited acts mentioned earlier from the beginning of the surah. ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden﴾: People have differed about what the major sins (kaba'ir) are. Ibn 'Abbas said: the major sins are every sin that Allah has concluded with a fire, a curse, or wrath. Ibn Mas'ud said: the major sins are the sins mentioned from the beginning of this surah up to the beginning of this verse. Some scholars said: everything that Allah is disobeyed in is a major sin, and some of them counted them as seventeen. In al-Bukhari, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Avoid the seven destructive sins: associating partners with Allah, sorcery, killing a soul, consuming usury, consuming the property of an orphan, fleeing on the day of the battle-line, and slandering chaste women." There is no doubt that these are among the major sins, given the explicit mention of them in the hadith. Some added other things to them, and the hadiths state explicitly that they are major sins, and the Qur'an or hadith contain threats against them. Among them are: disobedience to parents ('uquq al-walidayn), giving false testimony (shahadat al-zur), the perjurous oath (al-yamin al-ghamus), adultery (al-zina), theft (al-sariqa), drinking wine (shurb al-khamr), plundering (al-nahba), despairing of the mercy of Allah (al-qunut min rahmat Allah), feeling secure from the plan of Allah (al-amn min makr Allah), withholding water from the traveler (ibn al-sabil), desecration within the Sacred House (al-ilhad fi al-bayt al-haram), tale-bearing (al-namima), neglecting to guard against urine, misappropriation of booty (al-ghulul), a man's attacking the honor of his brother, and injustice in judgment. ﴿We will remove from you your misdeeds﴾: a promise of forgiveness of minor sins if major sins are avoided. ﴿A noble entrance﴾: "mudkhal" is a noun of place, and here it means Paradise.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 32:

﴿And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others.﴾ The occasion of its revelation: the women said, "If only we were equal to the men in inheritance, and we shared with them in military raiding (ghazw)." So it was revealed as a prohibition against that, because in their wishing there is a rejection of the ruling of the Shari'ah (sharī'ah, the divine law). Thus the prohibition includes wishing to oppose all the legal rulings of the Shari'ah. ﴿For men there is a share of what they have earned.﴾ That is, of reward and good deeds. It has also been said: of inheritance; but the word "earned" (iktisab) rejects this view.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 33:

﴿And for each We have appointed heirs to what is left by parents and close relatives﴾ [The verse itself]: Its meaning has two possibilities. The first: for every kind of property We have appointed heirs who inherit it, so "of what is left" is an explanation of "each." The second: for every person We have appointed heirs who inherit from what is left by parents and close relatives, so "of what is left" is in this case connected to a hidden verb. The "mawali" (heirs, i.e., the inheritors and the agnatic kinsmen, 'asabah) here means the heirs and the 'asabah.

﴿And to those with whom your oaths have bound you, give them their share﴾: Scholars differed as to whether it is abrogated (mansukhah) or effective (muhkamah). Those who said it is abrogated stated that its meaning is inheritance by the alliance that existed in the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period). It was also said that it refers to the brotherhood that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) established among his Companions. Then it was abrogated by: ﴿And blood relatives are more entitled to one another﴾ [al-Anfal: 75], so inheritance became for relatives. Those who said it is effective differed. Ibn 'Abbas said: it refers to support and assistance through the alliance, not inheritance through it. Abu Hanifah said: it concerns inheritance, and that if two men make one another their ally on the condition that they inherit from each other, that is valid, even if there is no kinship between them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 34:

﴿Men are the protectors and maintainers of women﴾ Qawwam (qawwām) is an intensive form (ṣīgha mubālagha) from al-qiyām ʿalā al-shayʾ, meaning to take charge of a thing and to have sole authority in managing it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Men are rulers (umarāʾ) over women." ﴿because of what Allah has given preference to some of them over others﴾ The bāʾ is causal (lil-taʿlīl), and mā is a verbal-noun (maṣdariyya) particle. The preference consists of leadership (al-imāma), jihad, the husband's control over divorce (malak al-ṭalāq), perfection of intellect, and other things. ﴿and because they spend of their wealth﴾ This refers to the dowry (al-ṣadaq) and the continuous maintenance (al-nafaqa al-mustamirra). ﴿So righteous women are devoutly obedient﴾ That is, righteous women who are upright in their religion are obedient to their husbands, or [it means] obedient to Allah in respect of their husbands' rights. ﴿guarding in the husband's absence what Allah has ordered them to guard﴾ That is, they guard everything that is hidden from their husband's knowledge, which includes guarding their own person, protecting his property and home, and keeping his secrets. ﴿with what Allah has guarded﴾ That is, by Allah's protection and care, or by His command to women that they obey their husbands and guard them; so mā is either a verbal-noun particle or means "that which." ﴿And those from whom you fear arrogance (nushūz)﴾ It has been said: the fear (khawf) here means certainty (yaqīn). ﴿then admonish them, and abandon them in the beds, and strike them﴾ These are kinds of disciplining a wife when she shows nushūz toward her husband, and they are graded: admonition for mild nushūz, abandonment for what is more serious than that, and striking for what is more serious still. Whenever she desists from nushūz by any form of discipline, one does not proceed to what comes after it. Abandonment here means ceasing to lie with her in the bed; it has also been said that it means ceasing intercourse while lying with her. The striking is non-severe (ghayr mubarriḥ). ﴿But if they obey you, then seek no means against them﴾ That is, if the wife obeys her husband, then he has no right to harm her by abandonment or striking.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 4, Verse 35:**

﴿And if you fear a breach between the two of them﴾. *Shiqaq* (discord, enmity, ill will). The original wording would have been "if you fear a breach between them," but the adverbial phrase was attributed to *shiqaq* by way of *ittisa'* (figurative extension, a rhetorical device), as in His saying, ﴿Rather, the scheming of night and day﴾ [Saba': 33]. The underlying sense is "scheming by night and day." ﴿Then send an arbitrator﴾, and so on. Here Allah mentions the arbitrator in the case of a wife's *nushuz* (disobedience, defiance of her husband), and the arbitrator in the case of her obedience. He then mentions here another situation: when relations between the spouses have deteriorated, the couple cannot be reconciled, and it is not known which of the two is the wrongdoer. Then two Muslim arbitrators are sent to examine their matter, and whatever separation they see fit, whether *talaq* (divorce) or *khul'* (divorce initiated by the wife through compensation), is enforced without the husband's permission. Abu Hanifa said: they have no authority to separate the spouses unless this authority is granted to them. If they disagree, nothing is binding except by their mutual agreement. The well-known position of the school of Malik is that the ruler (*hakim*) is the one who sends the two arbitrators. It was also said that the two spouses send them. In [the author's time], the custom of the judges was to send a trustworthy woman rather than two arbitrators. Some scholars said: "This is a change to the ruling of the Qur'an and the established Sunnah." ﴿from his family, and an arbitrator from her family﴾. It is permissible within the school that the two arbitrators be from outside the families of the spouses, but the more perfect course is that they be from their families, as Allah mentioned. ﴿If they both desire reconciliation, Allah will cause harmony between them﴾. The pronoun in *yuridaa* (they both desire) refers to the two arbitrators, and the pronoun in *baynahumaa* (between them) refers to the spouses, according to the more apparent view. It was also said that both pronouns refer to the spouses, and it was said that both refer to the arbitrators.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 36:

﴿And to the neighbor who is a relative, and to the neighbor who is a stranger﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The neighbor who is a relative" (al-jar dhi al-qurba) is the one near in lineage, and "the neighbor who is a stranger" (al-jar al-junub) is the non-relative. It was also said: "the neighbor who is a relative" is the one near in dwelling to you, and "al-junub" is the one far in dwelling from you. Some of them defined the extent of neighborhood (hadd al-jiwar) as forty cubits (dhira') in every direction.

﴿and the companion by your side﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: "the companion in travel" (al-rafiq fi al-sa'y). ʿAli ibn Abi Talib said: "the wife."

﴿mukhtalan﴾ is an active participle whose form is mufta'il, derived from al-khuyala', which is arrogance and a person's admiration of himself.

﴿fakhuran﴾ means exceedingly boastful.

Translation:

﴿Those who are miserly﴾ is either a substitute for the phrase "arrogant, boastful" (in the preceding verse), or in the accusative to express censure, or in the nominative by way of a suppressed subject (a predicate for an implied subject), or a subject whose predicate is omitted, its implied sense being "they will be punished." The verse was revealed concerning the Jews: it was sent down about a group among them, such as Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut, who used to say to the Ansar: "Do not spend your wealth on jihad and on charity." Yet it is also general in its application to those Muslims who commit these same deeds.

ِAnd those who spend their wealth to be seen by people"—this is coordinated with "those who are stingy," and it was said it is coordinated with "the disbelievers." The verse concerns the hypocrites who used to spend in zakat and jihad out of show (riya') and flattery (muṣāni'a). It was also said it concerns the Jews, and it was said it concerns the polytheists of Makkah who spent their wealth in fighting the Muslims. ﴿Qarīnan﴾ means a constant companion who leads him astray.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verses 39–40:

﴿And what would it harm them if they had believed in Allah and the Last Day?﴾ The verse: it is an invitation addressed to them in the manner of gentle persuasion, or a rebuke for abandoning faith and spending (in charity). It is as if He says: what harm would befall them in that?

﴿An atom's weight﴾ means its weight, and it is the small ant. This is an example with the little to alert to the much.

﴿And if it is a good deed﴾ — with the nominative (ḥasanatun) as the subject (fā'il), and takun being complete (tāmmah); and with the accusative (ḥasanatan) as the predicate (khabar), on the basis that it is incomplete (nāqisah), its subject being a pronoun hidden within it.

﴿He multiplies it﴾ means He increases it: the one who does one good deed is given tenfold up to seven hundred-fold or more.

﴿And gives from Himself a great reward﴾ means from His own presence, as a bounty and an addition beyond the reward of the deed.
