Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verses 41–42:

﴿فَكَيْفَ إِذَا جِئْنَا﴾ Its implied sense: How will it be when We bring ﴿from every nation a witness﴾ [a reference to the verse's opening]. ﴿بِشَهِيدٍ﴾ [a witness], who is their prophet, testifying against them regarding their deeds. ﴿وَجِئْنَا بِكَ عَلَىٰ هَـٰؤُلاۤءِ شَهِيداً﴾ [And We bring you as a witness against these], meaning you will bear witness against your people. When Ibn Mas'ud recited this verse to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), his eyes overflowed with tears. ﴿لَوْ تُسَوَّىٰ بِهِمُ ٱلأَرْضُ﴾ [Would that the earth were levelled over them], meaning they wish they could be buried in it, so that the earth would be levelled over them as it is over the dead. It was also said: they wish they were equal to the earth, like His saying: ﴿وَيَقُولُ ٱلْكَافِرُ يٰلَيْتَنِي كُنتُ تُرَاباً﴾ [And the disbelieving man will say: "Would that I were dust!"] (78:40). This is due to the horrors of the Day of Resurrection that they witness. ﴿وَلاَ يَكْتُمُونَ ٱللَّهَ حَدِيثاً﴾ [And they will not conceal from Allah any statement] — a resumed statement informing that on the Day of Resurrection they will not conceal anything from Allah. If it is asked: How is this consistent with their saying: ﴿وَٱللَّهِ رَبِّنَا مَا كُنَّا مُشْرِكِينَ﴾ [By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists] (6:23)? The answer is in two respects. First: concealment will not benefit them, for when they conceal, their limbs speak, so it is as though they had not concealed. Second: they are different groups, with different times. It was also said that His saying "and they will not conceal" is coordinated with "would be levelled" — meaning they wish they would not conceal, because if they concealed they would be disgraced.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verses 41–42:

﴿فَكَيْفَ إِذَا جِئْنَا﴾ Its implied sense: How will it be when We bring ﴿from every nation a witness﴾ [a reference to the verse's opening]. ﴿بِشَهِيدٍ﴾ [a witness], who is their prophet, testifying against them regarding their deeds. ﴿وَجِئْنَا بِكَ عَلَىٰ هَـٰؤُلاۤءِ شَهِيداً﴾ [And We bring you as a witness against these], meaning you will bear witness against your people. When Ibn Mas'ud recited this verse to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), his eyes overflowed with tears. ﴿لَوْ تُسَوَّىٰ بِهِمُ ٱلأَرْضُ﴾ [Would that the earth were levelled over them], meaning they wish they could be buried in it, so that the earth would be levelled over them as it is over the dead. It was also said: they wish they were equal to the earth, like His saying: ﴿وَيَقُولُ ٱلْكَافِرُ يٰلَيْتَنِي كُنتُ تُرَاباً﴾ [And the disbelieving man will say: "Would that I were dust!"] (78:40). This is due to the horrors of the Day of Resurrection that they witness. ﴿وَلاَ يَكْتُمُونَ ٱللَّهَ حَدِيثاً﴾ [And they will not conceal from Allah any statement] — a resumed statement informing that on the Day of Resurrection they will not conceal anything from Allah. If it is asked: How is this consistent with their saying: ﴿وَٱللَّهِ رَبِّنَا مَا كُنَّا مُشْرِكِينَ﴾ [By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists] (6:23)? The answer is in two respects. First: concealment will not benefit them, for when they conceal, their limbs speak, so it is as though they had not concealed. Second: they are different groups, with different times. It was also said that His saying "and they will not conceal" is coordinated with "would be levelled" — meaning they wish they would not conceal, because if they concealed they would be disgraced.

﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾. Its occasion of revelation (sabab) was that a group of the Companions drank wine before it was prohibited, then stood for prayer, and one of them led them and made mistakes in the recitation. So its meaning is the prohibition of prayer in a state of intoxication. Some people said: it has been abrogated (naskh) by the prohibition of wine. That does not follow, because it contains nothing that implies the permissibility of wine. It is only a prohibition of prayer in a state of intoxication, and that ruling holds both at the time when wine was permitted and at the time when it was prohibited. Others said: its meaning is, let there be no intoxication among you that prevents approaching prayer, since a person is commanded to pray, so it implies a prohibition of intoxication and of its cause, which is drinking. But this is far from the apparent sense of the wording. ﴿Until you know what you are saying﴾: until your intellects return to you and you know what you recite. It appears from this that intoxication is when a person does not know what he is saying. From this, some people derived that the intoxicated person's divorce and acknowledgment (iqrar) are not binding.

﴿Nor in a state of junub (major ritual impurity), except when passing through﴾: "nor junuban" is coordinated (ʿatf) upon the position of "while you are intoxicated," since that is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). Junub here means one who is not in a state of purity due to emission of semen or penetration, and it applies to a group, as is shown by the exception of the plural from it. There is disagreement regarding "passing through" (ʿabir sabil). It has been said that it refers to the traveller. The meaning of the verse on this view is: he forbade approaching prayer while junub, except while traveling, in which case one prays with tayammum (dry ablution) without ghusl (full bodily washing). The apparent sense of the verse is therefore the permissibility of tayammum for the junub while travelling, and the permissibility of tayammum for the junub while resident is derived from a hadith. It has also been said that "passing through" refers to one who crosses through the mosque, and "prayer" here means the mosque, because it is the place of prayer. The meaning of the verse on this view is: the junub is forbidden to approach the mosque except while passing through it. On this view al-Shafiʿi held that it is permissible for the junub to pass through the mosque but not to sit in it. Malik prohibited both passing through and sitting, while Dawud al-Zahiri permitted both.

﴿And if you are ill or on a journey﴾: the occasion of its revelation was that the Companions lacked water during the expedition of al-Muraysi, so tayammum was permitted to them for lack of water. Then, lack of water has three aspects. The first: its lack while travelling. The second: its lack during illness. Tayammum is permitted in these two aspects by consensus (ijmaʿ), because the verse is explicit regarding illness and travel when water is lacking in them, by His saying: ﴿And if you are ill or on a journey﴾, then He said: ﴿and you find no water﴾. The third aspect: lack of water while resident and not ill. The jurists differed regarding it. The school of Abu Hanifa holds that tayammum is not permitted in it, because the apparent sense of the verse is that lack of water is considered only together with illness or travel. The school of Malik and al-Shafiʿi holds that tayammum is permitted in it. If we say the verse does not imply this, its permissibility is derived from the Sunnah. If we say the verse does imply it, its permissibility is derived from it, and this is the more probable view, God willing. That is because He mentioned illness and travel at the beginning of the verse, then mentioned the breaking of ablution (hadath) without illness or travel, then after all that said: ﴿and you find no water﴾. So His saying ﴿and you find no water﴾ refers to the ill, to the traveller, and to one who has broken his ablution while neither ill nor travelling. On this view tayammum is permitted for one who lacks water while neither ill nor travelling, so the verse is a proof for Malik and al-Shafiʿi. In the school of Malik, tayammum is also permitted for the ill person who finds water but cannot use it because of harm to his body. If we say the verse does not imply this, its permissibility is derived from the Sunnah; and if we say the Sunnah implies it, its permissibility is derived from it, on the basis that His saying ﴿if you are ill﴾ means ill in a way that prevents you from touching water. The illness that permits tayammum according to Malik is that one fears death, or an increase of illness, or a delay in recovery. According to al-Shafiʿi it is only fear of death. The definition of travel is absence from one's home area, whether or not it is a journey in which prayer is shortened.

﴿Or one of you comes﴾: "or" here has two interpretations. The first: that it is for distinction and classification, in its proper function. The second: that it means "and" (waw). On the view that it is in its proper function, His saying "and you find no water" refers back to the ill, the traveller, the one who comes from the lavatory, and the one who has touched women, whether they are ill or travellers, or as we mentioned before. This implies the permissibility of tayammum for the resident who is healthy when he lacks water, which is the school of Malik and al-Shafiʿi, so the verse is a proof for them. On the view that it means "and," His saying "and you find no water" refers back to the ill and the traveller, which implies that tayammum is not permitted except in illness or travel when water is lacking, and that it is not permitted for the resident who is healthy when he lacks water; but its permissibility for him is derived from another source. The more probable view is that "or" is in its proper function, for two reasons. The first is that making it mean "and" removes it from its origin, and that is weak. The second is that if it is in its proper function, it carries the benefit of permitting tayammum for the resident who is healthy when he lacks water, according to what appears to us from it; whereas if it means "and," it does not yield this benefit. The argument of those who take it to mean "and" is that if it were in its proper function, the meaning would require that illness and travel are a cause of breaking ablution like the lavatory, because it is coordinated with them. But this does not follow, because coordination with "or" here is for classification and distinction. The meaning of the verse is as if He said: tayammum is permitted for you if you find no water, if you are ill or on a journey, or if you have broken your ablution while neither ill nor travelling.

﴿Al-ghaʾit (the lavatory)﴾: its original meaning is a low-lying place. Here it is a metaphor (kinaya) for the impurity that comes out of the two passages, namely excrement, wind, and urine, because whoever goes to the ghaʾit has these three kinds of breaking of ablution. It has also been said that it is a metaphor only for excrement, and that the obligation of ablution for urine and wind is derived from the Sunnah. The same applies to wadi (a whitish fluid after urination) and madhi (a clear fluid of arousal).

﴿Or you have touched women﴾: scholars differed regarding the intended meaning of "touching" (mulamasa) here, in three views. The first: that it is sexual intercourse and whatever is less than it, such as kissing and touching with the hand or other parts; this is the view of Malik. On this view, ablution is broken by touching that is less than intercourse, with detail in the school's position, and tayammum is obligatory with it if water is lacking, and the junub is among those who may perform tayammum. The second view: that it is whatever is less than intercourse. On this view, ablution is broken by touching, and tayammum is not permitted for the junub. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab held this view, and its permissibility is derived from a hadith. The third: that it is intercourse. On this view tayammum is permitted for the junub, and what is less than intercourse does not break ablution; this is the view of Abu Hanifa.

﴿And you find no water﴾: this indicates the obligation to seek water, which is the view of Malik, contrary to Abu Hanifa. If one finds water for a price, scholars differed on whether he may perform tayammum or not. If it is given to him as a gift, they differed on whether he must accept it or not.

﴿Then perform tayammum﴾: tayammum linguistically means intention (qasd), and in jurisprudence it means purification with earth. It has been transferred from its linguistic meaning.

﴿With clean earth (sa'id tayyiban)﴾: according to Malik, al-Sa'id is the surface of the earth, whether it is dust, sand, or stones, so he permitted tayammum with all of that. According to al-Shafiʿi it is dust only. Tayyib here means pure. Scholars differed regarding tayammum with minerals such as gold, with salt, with dust that has been transported, such as that placed in a tray, with baked brick, with plaster that has been fired, with a wall, and with plants growing on the surface of the earth. All of this is based on the disagreement over the meaning of al-sa'id.

﴿Then wipe your faces and your hands﴾: tayammum is only in these two limbs. The face is mentioned before the hands, following the apparent sense of the verse, and that is recommended (nadb) according to Malik. The face is wiped completely. As for the hands, scholars differed on whether one wipes them up to the wrists (kawʿayn) or up to the elbows. The wording of the verse is open to both, because it did not specify a limit. Those who said "up to the elbows" argued that this is unrestricted and so should be interpreted in light of the restricted case, which is its limit in ablution by the elbows.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 44:

﴿Those who were given a portion of the Scripture﴾ are the Jews here. As for the second occurrence, al-Suhayli said: the first passage was revealed concerning Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut, and the second was revealed concerning Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. ﴿They purchase error﴾ is an expression for their preferring disbelief over faith. So "purchase" (al-shira') is used metaphorically, as in His saying: "They have bought error in exchange for guidance." And in the repetition of His saying ﴿Sufficient is Allah﴾ there is emphasis (mubalaghah).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 46:

﴿Among those who are Jews﴾ — whether this refers back to "those who were given a portion" (alladhina utu nasiban), or to "your enemies," it is an explanation (bayan). Al-Farisi said: it is the beginning of a statement, its implied meaning being: "Among those who are Jews, there are a people..." It was also said: it is connected to "nasiran" (a helper), according to the view of al-Farisi. ﴿They distort the words﴾ — this may mean distorting the wording or the meaning. It was also said: "al-kalim" here refers to the Torah, and it was said: it refers to the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿Without being heard﴾ — its meaning: "May you not hear anything." ﴿Ra'ina﴾ — this was mentioned in al-Baqarah [104]. ﴿We hear and we obey﴾ — this is a substitute for their saying: "We hear and we disobey." "Isma'" (listen) is a substitute for their saying: "Isma' ghayra musma'" (listen, may you not be made to hear). "Unzurna" (look at us) is a substitute for their saying: "Ra'ina," and it means "look" or "wait." So these three things stand in contrast to the three things for which He censured them when they said them, because of the bad manners they contain toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He informed that if they had said these other three in place of those, it would have been better for them, for these contain no bad manners.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 47:

﴿Muṣaddiqan﴾ (confirming): mentioned in al-Baqarah. ﴿An naṭmisa wujūhan﴾ (that We obliterate faces). Ibn ʿAbbas said: their obliteration is that the eyes are removed from them and they are turned back to the nape, so that this is a reversal of the rear (al-dabr). It was also said: their obliteration is the erasing of the outlines of their forms, of nose, eye or brow, until they become like the backs (adbār) in being empty of the senses. ﴿Aw nalʿanahum﴾ (or We curse them), i.e., We transform them (namsakhahum) as We transformed the People of the Sabbath (aṣḥāb al-sabt), which has been mentioned in al-Baqarah. Or it may be from the well-known cursing (al-laʿn al-maʿrūf), and the pronoun refers to the faces, the intended meaning being their owners, or it refers to those who were given the Book, as an iltifat (shift in grammatical person).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 48:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾. This verse is the decisive one in the matter of the threat (al-wa'id). It clarifies what conflicts among the verses on this subject, it is the proof for the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah), and it is decisive against the Kharijites (al-Khawarij), the Mu'tazilah, and the Murji'ah. The doctrine of the People of the Sunnah is that sinful believers are subject to Allah's will: if He wills, He punishes them, and if He wills, He forgives them. Their proof is this verse, for it is explicit in this meaning. The doctrine of the Kharijites is that sinners will certainly be punished, whether their sins are minor or major. The doctrine of the Mu'tazilah is that they will certainly be punished for major sins. Against both groups stands His saying: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that﴾. The doctrine of the Murji'ah is that all sinners will certainly be forgiven, and that no sin harms a person who has faith. Their view is refuted by the phrase "for whom He wills," which is a restriction applying to some sinners. The Mu'tazilah interpreted the verse according to their doctrine, saying: "for whom He wills" refers to the one who repents, about whom there is no disagreement that he will not be punished. This interpretation is far-fetched, because His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ refers to someone who has not repented from shirk, and likewise His saying "And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills" refers to someone who has not repented from disobedience, so that the beginning and end of the verse follow one pattern. The Murji'ah interpreted it according to their doctrine, saying: "for whom He wills" means "for whom He wills to believe." This too is far-fetched, as the wording does not require it. There are many verses in the Qur'an concerning the threat. The Mu'tazilah applied them to sinners, the Murji'ah applied them to disbelievers, and the People of the Sunnah applied them to disbelievers and to sinners whom Allah does not forgive, just as they applied the verses of promise to believers who did not sin, to sinners who repented, and to sinners who did not repent but whom Allah forgives. Thus, according to the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah, no contradiction remains between the verse of promise and the verse of threat; rather, their meanings are combined. This is unlike the view of others, for the verses conflict in their view. The summary of the doctrines is this: if a disbeliever repents from his disbelief, he is forgiven by consensus; if he dies in his disbelief, he is not forgiven and abides in the Fire by consensus. As for a sinful believer, if he repents, he is forgiven; if he dies without repentance, this is the matter over which people have differed.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 49:

﴿Those who justify themselves﴾ are the Jews, may Allah curse them. Their self-justification is their saying: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved." It was also said: it is their praising of themselves. ﴿Not a fatil (a thread)﴾. The fatil is the thread in the split of a date-stone. It was also said: it is what comes out between your two fingers and palm when you twist them together. This is a figure of speech and an expression for the least of things, so that it indicates the greater by way of a fortiori reasoning.

﴿They fabricate﴾ is evidence that their self-praise is based on falsehood. ﴿They believe in al-Jibt (idols, or sorcery and false powers) and al-Taghut (every transgressor or false object of worship)﴾. Ibn Abbas said: al-Jibt is Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and al-Taghut is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. Umar ibn al-Khattab said: al-Jibt is sorcery, and al-Taghut is Satan. It was also said: al-Jibt is the soothsayer (kahin), and al-Taghut is the sorcerer. In summary, both terms refer to everything that is worshipped or obeyed besides Allah. ﴿And they say to those who disbelieve﴾ (the verse). Its occasion of revelation: Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, or others among the Jews, said to the disbelievers of Quraysh: "You are better guided on the path than Muhammad and his companions."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verses 53–54:

﴿Do they have a share of the kingdom?﴾ The hamza here is an interrogative particle carrying the sense of denial.

﴿Naqir﴾ (the naqir) is the small hollow in the back of a date pit. This is a figure of speech, expressing the least of things. The intended meaning is to describe the Jews as stingy: were they to have a share of the kingdom, they would withhold even the naqir, which is the least of things, and they would withhold what is greater than it all the more so.

﴿Or do they envy the people?﴾ He describes them with envy alongside stinginess. Here "the people" refers to the Prophet ﷺ and his community, and the "bounty" is prophethood. It has also been said that the bounty is victory and honour, and it has also been said that "the people" are the Arabs and the bounty is the Prophet ﷺ being from among them.

﴿Indeed, We gave the family of Abraham the Book and wisdom﴾ By the family of Abraham is meant his descendants, including the Children of Israel and others whom God granted the books He sent down and the wisdom He taught. The purpose of the verse is to refute the Jews in their envy of our master Muhammad ﷺ. Its meaning is a challenge to them based on what they themselves recognise of God's exalted bounty upon the family of Abraham: so why do you single out Muhammad ﷺ for envy, rather than others upon whom God has bestowed His favour?

﴿A great kingdom﴾ The kingdom among the family of Abraham is the kingdom of Joseph, David and Solomon.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 55–57:

﴿Among them are those who believed in him﴾ etc. It has been said: what is meant by "among the Jews" is those who believed in the Prophet (ﷺ), or in the Qur'an mentioned in His saying, Most High: ﴿confirming what is with you﴾, or in what was mentioned of the story of Ibrahim (Abraham). So these are three possible interpretations of the pronoun in "in him." It has also been said: "among them" means among the family of Ibrahim (Abraham), those who believed in Ibrahim, and among them are those who disbelieved, like His saying, Most High: ﴿Among them are the guided, but many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Hadid: 26]. 

﴿Every time their skins are roasted through﴾ etc. It has been said: new skins will be substituted for them after other skins, since it is their souls that are being punished. It has also been said: the changing of the skins means changing their attributes by the Fire. It has been said: "the skins" refers to garments (sarabil), but this is far-fetched.

﴿purified spouses﴾ This was mentioned in al-Baqarah.

﴿a shade, extended﴾: the adjective "extended" (zalil) is derived from the same root as "shade" (zill), for emphasis, meaning: lasting, not abolished by the sun. It has also been said: it means the absence of heat and cold.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verses 58–59:

﴿Indeed, Allah commands you﴾ etc. It is said that it is addressed to the rulers (wulat), and it is said: to the Prophet (ﷺ), when he took the key of the Ka'bah from Uthman ibn Talhah. Its wording is general, and so is its ruling. ﴿And those in authority among you﴾ are: the rulers. It is said: they are the scholars. It was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Hudhafah, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent in a military detachment (sariyyah). ﴿Then refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾: referring it back to Allah is examining His Book (kitab), and referring it back to the Messenger (ﷺ) is asking him during his lifetime and examining his Sunnah (sunnah, the prophetic practice) after his death. ﴿If you should be believers﴾: this condition may refer back to his saying "then refer it back," or to his saying "obey," and the first is more apparent, because it is closer to it. ﴿And better in result (ta'wil)﴾: that is, better in outcome and consequence. It is also said: better in judgment than you.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verses 66–69:

﴿And if We had decreed for them﴾ The verse means: if there were imposed upon them what was imposed upon those before them of hardships, they would not do it, owing to the weakness of their submission, except a few of them, who are truly believers. It has been related that among these few were Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿud, ʿAmmar ibn Yasir and Thabit ibn Qays. ﴿except a few﴾ is in the nominative (rafʿ) as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun implied in the verb. Ibn ʿAmir alone read it in the accusative (naṣb), according to the original form of the exception (asl al-istithna'), or as "except doing a little" (illa fiʿlan qalilan). ﴿what they were admonished with﴾ i.e., following the Prophet ﷺ, obeying him and submitting to him. ﴿and firmer in establishment﴾ i.e., more affirming of their faith. ﴿And then We would surely give them﴾ is the answer to an assumed question about their condition if they had done that. ﴿then they will be with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favor﴾ is a reward for obedience, meaning they will be with them in Paradise. This verse explains His saying, the Exalted: ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾ [al-Fatiha: 7]. The ṣiddiq (truthful one) is on the pattern of fiʿil (fiʿīl) derived from truthfulness (ṣidq) and from affirming (taṣdiq), and it is meant as an intensive form. The ṣiddiqun are the highest of people in rank after the prophets; the martyrs (shuhada') are those slain in the way of Allah, and whoever is in their category among the rest of the martyrs, such as the one drowned and the one killed by a collapsing building, as stated in the hadith that they are seven. ﴿And excellent are those as companions﴾ The reference is to the four categories mentioned. The word rafiq (companion) applies to the singular and the plural, like khalit, and it is a singular noun denoting a collective genus. The meaning of the statement is information and an incitement to the obedience through which companionship with these people is attained.

﴿That is the bounty﴾. The reference is to the reward for obedience, namely companionship with those mentioned in Paradise. Al-fadl (the bounty) is either an adjective or a khabar (predicate).

﴿Take your precautions﴾, i.e., be on guard against your enemy and prepare for them.

﴿Then go forth in separate groups﴾, i.e., go out to jihad in scattered companies. This is a metaphor (kināyah) for raiding parties (sarāyā). It was said that a thubah is more than ten. Its form is فَعَلَة with a fatḥah on the ʿayn, and its final radical (lām) is elided.

﴿Or go forth all together﴾, i.e., assembled in one massive army. So He gave them the choice of going out to battle in small or large numbers.

﴿And indeed among you is one who will certainly lag behind﴾. The address is to the believers, and what is meant by "one" (man) is the hypocrites. They are expressed as "among you" because they claim to be among the believers and say, "We believe." The lām in لمن is for emphasis, and in لَيُبَطِّئَنَّ it is the answer to an omitted oath (qasam). Its meaning: he slows others down, discouraging them from jihad and leading them to stay behind from the raid. It was also said: يُبَطِّئ means that he himself lags behind from the raid and is sluggish.

﴿If a calamity strikes you﴾, i.e., killing and defeat. The meaning is that the hypocrite is pleased by his absence from the believers when they are defeated. Shahīdan (present) means present with them.

﴿And if bounty from God comes to you﴾, i.e., victory and booty. The meaning is that the hypocrite regrets not having gone out with them when they gain booty, so he wishes he had been with them.

﴿as if there had never been any affection between you and him﴾. This is a parenthetical clause (jumlat iʿtirāḍ) between the governing element (al-ʿāmil) and its governed element (maʿmūl), so it is not permissible to pause at it. This affection is in the hypocrite's outward appearance, not in his belief.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verses 74–76:

﴿Those who sell﴾ i.e., who sell (yabī'ūn) [the life of this world for the Hereafter], ﴿and then he is killed or he is victorious﴾. He mentioned the two situations of the fighter and promised a reward for each of them. ﴿And what is with you that you do not fight?﴾ This is an exhortation to fighting. Ma (what) is the subject (mubtada'), and lakum (for you), the prepositional phrase, is the predicate (khabar). "Wa-la tuqatilūn" (and you do not fight) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). Al-mustad'afīn (the oppressed) are those whom the polytheists of Quraysh confined in Makkah in order to tempt them away from Islam; it is coordinated with the word "Allah" (in the phrase "in the way of Allah"), or it is an object of accompaniment (maf'ūl ma'ahu). ﴿Of the city whose people are wrongdoers﴾ is Makkah when it was under the polytheists. ﴿Who fight in the way of Allah﴾ and what follows is a statement of information, intended to strengthen the hearts of the Muslims and to urge them to fight.

The verse "Those to whom it was said, 'Restrain your hands'" and what follows. It is said: it refers to a group of the Companions who had been ordered to refrain from fighting before jihad was made obligatory. They wished that they would be commanded to it, but when they were commanded, they disliked it. This was not from doubt about their religion, but from fear of death. ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾. This verse is among the virtues of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). His obedience was like the obedience of Allah only because he commands and forbids on behalf of Allah. ﴿And whoever turns away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾. That is, whoever turns away from obeying you, you are not a guardian over him to protect his deeds. Rather, his reckoning and recompense are with Allah. In this is a disengagement and a truce, which is abrogated (mansūkh, superseded by a later ruling, from naskh) by fighting.

"And they say, 'Obedience.'" That is, our affair and our matter is obedience to you; and this is said of the hypocrites, by consensus. "But when they leave you, a group of them plot by night other than what you say." Bayyata means they devise the matter at night. The pronoun in "taqulu" refers to the addressee, who is the Prophet (ﷺ), or it refers to the group. "So turn away from them," that is, do not punish them.

Surah 4, verse 82 in the commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil):

﴿Will they not then reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ He urges reflection on its meanings so that its proofs and evidences become apparent. ﴿Much contradiction﴾: that is, contradiction as is found in human speech, or variation in eloquence. But the Qur'an is free of that, which indicates that it is the speech of God. If a doubt befalls anyone and he thinks there is contradiction in some part of the Qur'an, then it is obligatory that he suspect his own reasoning, ask the people of knowledge (ahl al-'ilm), and consult their works, until he knows that this is not a contradiction.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 83:

﴿And when there comes to them a matter of security or fear, they spread it abroad.﴾ It is said: they are the hypocrites (munafiqun). It is also said: they are a group of the weaker Muslims, who, whenever news reached them about the expeditions (sarayا) and armies or other matters, would spread it abroad, meaning they spoke of it and publicized it before knowing whether it was true. Their spreading of it caused harm to the Muslims, along with the hastiness and lack of verification involved in that, so God rebuked them for it. ﴿And if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, those among them who seek to derive it would have known it.﴾ That is: if these people had refrained from speaking about that matter that had reached them, and had referred it to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and to those in authority (uli al-amr), who are the senior Companions and the people of insight among them, then those people who seek to derive (yastanbitunahu), meaning who extract it, would have known it from the Messenger and those in authority. According to this view, those who seek to derive it are a group of Muslims who ask the Messenger (ﷺ) and those in authority about it. The preposition in His saying "yastanbitunahu, from them" (minhum) indicates the starting point (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), and it is connected to the verb, while the pronoun in the genitive refers to the Messenger and those in authority. It is also said: those who seek to derive it are the people in authority (uli al-amr), as came in the hadith from ʿUmar (raḍiya Allahu ʿanhu) that he heard that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had divorced his wives, so he entered upon him and said: "Did you divorce your wives?" He said: "No." So he stood at the door of the mosque and said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) has not divorced his wives." So God revealed this account. He said: "And I am the one who derived it." Accordingly, those who derive it are the people in authority, and the pronoun in the genitive refers to them, and "minhum" is explanatory of the kind (li-bayan al-jins). The deriving of it, on this view, is their asking the Prophet (ﷺ) about it, or by reflection and inquiry. The deriving of it under the first interpretation, which is asking the Messenger (ﷺ) and those in authority, is by those who spread it. ﴿And were it not for the grace of God upon you and His mercy⦆ That is: His guidance and His success, or His sending of the messengers and His sending down of the Books. The address in this verse is to the believers. ﴿except a few﴾ That is: except for a few instances of following. So the exception is from the verbal noun (masdar), and the meaning is: were it not for the grace and mercy of God, you would have followed Satan except in a few matters in which you would not have followed him. It is also said that it is an exception from the subject of "you followed" (ittaba'tum), meaning "except a few of you," and this is what the wording indicates; they are those who were not followers of Satan before Islam, such as Waraqah ibn Nawfal. The grace and mercy refer to the sending of the Messenger and the sending down of the Book. It is also said that the exception is from His saying "they spread it abroad."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 84:

﴿Thou art not charged except with thyself﴾. When some people held back from fighting, this was addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ); meaning: if they leave you alone, and you fight by yourself, then the responsibility falls only on you. ﴿And urge the believers﴾, meaning: concerning the believers, you have no obligation except to urge them. ﴿Perhaps Allah will restrain the might of those who disbelieve﴾. It has been said: "perhaps" (ʿasā) from Allah is binding. And "those who disbelieve" here refers to the Quraysh; Allah restrained them by their defeat at Badr and other battles, and by the conquest of Makkah. ﴿And Allah is greater in might and greater in punishment﴾, meaning: greater in retribution and torment.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 85:

﴿a good intercession﴾ is intercession on behalf of a Muslim to relieve him of distress, to ward off an injustice, or to bring him some benefit. A bad intercession is the opposite of that. It has also been said: the good intercession is obedience, and the bad intercession is disobedience. The first view (that it is intercession for others) is more apparent. The *kifl* (a share, or portion) is the *nasīb* (allotted share). ﴿Muqītan (sustaining, or watchful over all things)﴾. It has been said: powerful. It has been said: watchful. It has been said: one who sustains living creatures, meaning, one who provides them with their sustenance.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 86:

﴿So greet with a better greeting than it, or return it.﴾ The meaning of this is the command to return the greeting, and the option between returning it with the like of what was used to greet you, or with something better than it. The better is more excellent, such as when one is told, "Peace be upon you," and he returns the greeting while adding "and the mercy and blessings" (of Allah). Returning the greeting is an obligation upon the community as a collective duty (wajib 'ala al-kifayah) according to Malik and al-Shafi'i. Some people said it is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn). There is a difference of opinion regarding returning the greeting to the disbelievers. It was said: it is returned to them, based on the generality of the verse. It was said: it is not returned to them. And it was said: they are told "'alaykum" (upon you), in accordance with what has come in the hadith, and this is the position of Malik. And they are not initiated with the greeting.

Translation:

﴿Surely He will gather you﴾ is the response to an implied oath, and it contains the meaning of "gathering" (al-hashr), which is why it takes "ila" (to). ﴿And who is more truthful﴾: its wording is interrogative, but its meaning is that none is more truthful than Allah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 88:

﴿So what is wrong with you that you have become two groups concerning the hypocrites?﴾ "Ma" here is interrogative, meaning rebuke (al-tawbikh), and the address is to the Muslims. The meaning of "fi'atayn" is two differing groups (ta'ifatayn mukhtalifatayn), and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). The hypocrites intended here, according to Ibn 'Abbas, are a people who were in Makkah with the polytheists. They claimed to have believed but did not emigrate. Then some of them travelled to al-Sham for trade, and the Muslims disagreed: should they fight them and seize their merchandise, since they had not emigrated, or should they leave them alone, since they were believers? Zayd ibn Thabit said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites who turned back from fighting on the day of Uhud, and the Companions differed about their affair. This is refuted by His saying: ﴿until they emigrate﴾. ﴿Arkasahum﴾ means He misguided them and destroyed them.

**Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 4, verses 89–90:**

﴿They wish that you would disbelieve﴾: The pronoun refers to the hypocrites, meaning they wish that you would disbelieve.

﴿So take them﴾: he means by this capture.

﴿Except those who join﴾ (the verse): This is an exception from His saying ﴿So take them and kill them﴾. Its meaning is: whoever among the disbelievers who are not under treaty reaches (joins) disbelievers who are under treaty, meaning those between whom and the Muslims there is a covenant and truce, his ruling is the same as theirs in peace and in refraining from fighting him. This was at the beginning of Islam, and it was then abrogated (naskh) by fighting in the opening of Surah al-Bara'a (Surah 9). Al-Suhayli and others said: those who join are the Banu Mudlij ibn Kinana.

﴿to a people between you and whom there is a covenant﴾: the Banu Khuza'a. The Banu Mudlij entered into the truce of the Banu Khuza'a with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so the meaning of "join a people" is: they arrive at them and enter into what they have entered into of truce. It was also said: the meaning of "join" is "be related", but this is very weak, by the evidence of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) fighting against the Quraysh, who were his relatives and the relatives of the believers; how then would the relatives of the treaty-bound disbelievers not be fought?

﴿Or they come to you, their breasts constricted﴾: this is conjoined to "join" or to the description of "a people", which is: "between you and whom there is a covenant". The meaning varies according to that, and the first is more apparent. "Their breasts constricted" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), by the evidence of Ya'qub's reading "ḥaṣirat". Its meaning is: they were too constrained to fight and disliked it. The verse was revealed concerning a people who came to the Muslims and disliked fighting the Muslims, and also disliked fighting their own people, their disbelieving relatives, so Allah commanded restraint from them. This too was later abrogated by fighting.

﴿And if they withdraw from you﴾: meaning, if they make peace with you, then do not fight them. Here "al-salam" means submission.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 91:

﴿You will find others who wish to be secure from you and secure from their own people. Whenever they are returned to temptation, they plunge into it﴾: It was revealed concerning a group of deceivers, from the tribes of Asad and Ghatafan. When they came to Medina, they professed Islam and made covenants so that they would be safe from the Muslims. When they returned to their own people, they disbelieved and broke their covenants so that they would be safe from their own people. Here, *fitnah* (trial, or in this context, tempting disbelief) means disbelief according to the most apparent view. It was also said that it means testing.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 92:

﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake.﴾ It was revealed concerning the killing of al-Harith ibn Zayd by ʿAyyash ibn Rabiʿah. al-Harith had been tormenting him for his Islam. Then al-Harith embraced Islam and emigrated, but ʿAyyash did not know of his Islam, so he killed him. It was also said: the exception here is disjunctive (munqati, i.e. not from the same category as what precedes it), and the meaning is: it is not lawful for a believer to kill a believer in any way, but mistake may occur. The sound view is that it is connected (muttasil), and the meaning is: it is not proper for a believer, nor becoming of him, to kill a believer by way of mistake, without intention or transgression, since he is overcome in it. The accusative of khata' (mistake) is either a object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), or a circumstantial state (hal), or a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun (masdar mahdhuf).

﴿And whoever kills a believer by mistake, [the expiation is] the freeing of a believing slave and a compensation (diyah)﴾. This explains what is obligatory upon the one who kills by mistake: Allah made obligatory upon him the freeing (of a slave) and the blood-money (diyah). As for the freeing, it is from the killer's property; as for the blood-money, it is from the property of his ʿaqilah (the paternal kin who bear such obligations). This came from the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is an explanation of the verse, since its wording admits of this or of something else. The jurists agreed upon it. Malik stipulated for the slave to be freed that she be a believer, free of any contract of manumission (ʿaqd min ʿuqud al-hurriyyah), and free of defects. As for her being a believer, it is explicitly stated here, and therefore the scholars agreed upon it here; they differed regarding the expiation for zihar and the expiation for oaths. As for her being free of contracts of manumission, it is apparent from the words of the Exalted: ﴿the freeing of a slave﴾, because its apparent meaning is that it is an initiation of manumission when expiating by it. As for her being free of defect, they claimed that the unqualified mention of "slave" requires it, but there is room for examination in that.

The amount of the diyah is not specified in the verse. According to Malik it is one hundred camels for the people of camels, one thousand legal dinars for the people of gold, and twelve thousand legal dirhams for the people of silver. This is narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab.

﴿delivered to his family﴾, meaning handed over to them. "The family" here means the heirs. It is disputed over the period of its payment: it was said it is due immediately upon them; it was said they pay it over three years; it was said over four. The wording of "delivering" is unrestricted, and it is more apparent for immediacy, were it not for what came in the Sunnah concerning this.

﴿unless they remit it as charity﴾. The pronoun refers to the victim's guardians (awliya'), meaning: if they drop the diyah, it is dropped; and if the victim himself drops it, it is also dropped according to Malik and the majority, contrary to the Zahiriyyah. Their argument is that the pronoun refers to the guardians. The majority said: this applies only if the victim did not drop it.

﴿And if he was from a people hostile to you and he is a believer, then [the expiation is] the freeing of a believing slave﴾. The meaning of the verse: if the one killed by mistake was a believer whose people were disbelievers and enemies, those being combatants, then in his killing there is only the freeing (of a slave), not the diyah, so it is not paid to them, lest they strengthen themselves thereby against the Muslims. Ibn ʿAbbas held that this applies only to one who embraced Islam but remained in the land of war without emigrating; others disagreed with him. Malik held that in this case the diyah goes to the public treasury (bayt al-mal), so the verse is, in his view, abrogated (mansukhah).

﴿And if he was from a people between you and them is a covenant﴾. The verse means: if the one killed by mistake was from a people who were disbelievers bound by a treaty, then for such a person there is the freeing of a slave, and the diyah is delivered to his family because of their covenant. The victim in this case is a believer, and therefore Malik said: there is no expiation for killing a dhimmi. It was also said: the one killed in this verse is a disbeliever, and on this view expiation is obligatory for killing a dhimmi. It was also said: it is general, covering both believer and disbeliever, and the wording of the verse is unrestricted, except that its restriction is his words "and he is a believer" in the preceding verse. Al-Hasan recited here "and he is a believer."

﴿So whoever does not find [a slave], then fasting two consecutive months﴾, meaning: whoever does not find the freeing and is unable to obtain it, then fasting two consecutive months is a substitute for it.

﴿as a acceptance of repentance from Allah﴾. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), and its meaning is mercy from Him and lightening.

﴿Whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, to abide therein﴾ – the verse. It was revealed concerning Miqyas ibn Subaba, who had taken the blood-money (diyya) for his brother Hisham, who had been killed by mistake. He then killed a man of the people who had killed his brother, and he apostatized and became a polytheist. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered his execution. The position relied upon by the majority (jumhur) is that intentional killing is the deliberate taking of life with an iron implement, a stone, a stick, or other such means. This verse is inoperative according to the school of the Ash'ariyya (Ash'arites) and others who say that the sinful believers do not abide eternally in the Fire. The Mu'tazila and others who hold that sinners abide in the Fire have used it as proof, based on His words: "abiding therein." The Ash'ariyya have interpreted it in four ways. First, they said it refers to a disbeliever who kills a believer. Second, they said that "intentionally" here means one who regards killing as lawful, and that this leads to disbelief. Third, they said that "abiding therein" does not mean everlasting eternal duration, but is an expression for a long period. Fourth, they said that it has been abrogated (mansukha) by His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 116]. The Mu'tazila, however, took it at its apparent meaning and held that it abrogates (nasikh) His words: ﴿and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 116]. They argued for this with the statement of Zayd ibn Thabit: "The severe was revealed after the lenient," and with the statement of Ibn 'Abbas: "Whoever dies upon polytheism or killing abides eternally," and with the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Every sin, Allah may forgive it, except a man who dies a disbeliever, or a man who kills a believer intentionally." The verse and these reports indicate that killing has a specific ruling that distinguishes it from all other sins. The people differed concerning the one who killed intentionally if he repents: is his repentance accepted or not? Likewise, Ibn Rushd reported the disagreement concerning the killer who is subjected to retaliation (qisas): does the punishment in the Hereafter fall from him or not? The sound view is that it does fall from him, based on the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Whoever commits a sin and is punished for it in this world, it is an expiation (kaffara) for him." This is the view of the majority of scholars.

﴿When you travel in the way of Allah﴾ – that is, when you journey out to jihad. ﴿Then verify (fa-tabayyanu)﴾ – from bayan (clarification). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with the letter thaʼ (ث), from thabat (firmness), and the verb form tafa''ala here carries the sense of istaf'ala, meaning: seek to clarify the matter and establish it. ﴿Does not say to you "peace" (al-salam)﴾ – without an alif, meaning: he submitted and threw down his hand. Nafi' and others read al-salam, meaning greeting (tahiyya). It was revealed concerning a detachment (sariyya) that met a man, and he greeted them with peace and said: "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." One of them attacked him and killed him. This grieved the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The killer was 'Alam ibn Juthama and the one killed was 'Amir ibn al-Aghbat. It was said that the killer was Usama ibn Zayd and the one killed was Mirdas ibn Nahik. ﴿You seek the goods of the worldly life﴾ – meaning the spoils of war (ghanima), and the killed man had had flocks. ﴿With Allah are abundant spoils﴾ – a promise and a discouragement from seeking the spoils of one who has openly professed Islam. ﴿Thus you were before﴾ – it was said: its meaning is that you were disbelievers, and Allah guided you to Islam. It was also said: you used to conceal your faith from your people. ﴿Then Allah conferred favour upon you﴾ – with honour and victory, until you made it manifest.

The position relied upon by the majority (jumhur) is that intentional killing is the deliberate taking of life with an iron implement, a stone, a stick, or other such means. Third, they said that "abiding therein" does not mean everlasting eternal duration, but is an expression for a long period. Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 100:

﴿مُرَٰغَماً﴾ means a place of departure or refuge, a place where one humiliates (yurghim) his enemy by going to it. ﴿وَسَعَةً﴾ means abundance in the earth; it is also said: abundance in provision. ﴿فَقَدْ وَقَعَ أَجْرُهُ عَلىَ ٱللَّهِ﴾ means his reward has become fixed and established. ﴿وَمَن يَخْرُجْ مِن بَيْتِهِ﴾ — the ruling of this verse is general (in application). It was revealed concerning Damrah ibn al-Qays, who was among the oppressed (mustad'afin) in Makkah. He was sick, and when he heard what Allah had revealed about emigration (hijrah), he said: "Take me out." A bed was prepared for him and he was placed upon it and carried out, but he died on the way. It is also said that it was revealed concerning Khalid ibn Hizam, who emigrated toward the land of Abyssinia (al-Habashah), and a snake bit him on the way, so he died before he reached the land of Abyssinia.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary on Surah an-Nisa', verse 101:

﴿And when you travel through the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer, if you fear that those who disbelieve may tempt you.﴾ The scholars have differed in interpreting it, giving five opinions. The first is that it refers to shortening the four-rak'ah prayer (salah) to two rak'ahs while travelling, and therefore shortening is permitted only in a state of fear, according to the apparent meaning of the verse. This is the view of 'Aisha and 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with them both. The second is that the verse implies this, but shortening the prayer while travelling without fear is taken from the Sunnah. This is supported by the hadith of Ya'la ibn Umayya, who said: "I said to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Allah says, "if you fear," and people are now safe.' He said, 'I was amazed at what amazed you, so I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and he said: It is a charity which Allah has given you, so accept His charity.'" It is also established that the Prophet (ﷺ) shortened the prayer while travelling when he was safe. The third is that His words "if you fear" refer back to the verse that follows, "and when you are among them," and that the waw is extra; but this is far-fetched. The fourth is that the verse concerns the prayer of fear, according to the view of those who hold that each group prays one rak'ah separately. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The prayer was prescribed as four rak'ahs in residence, two rak'ahs while travelling, and one rak'ah in fear." The fifth is that the verse concerns the prayer during close combat (musayafa), so shortening in this case refers to the form of the prayer, like His words: "then if you fear, pray on foot or riding." 

If we say the verse concerns shortening while travelling, its apparent meaning is that shortening is a concession (rukhsah), while completing the prayer is better. This is the position of al-Shafi'i. Malik said that shortening is better. It is also said that the two are equal. Abu Hanifa held that shortening is obligatory. The wording of the verse does not indicate the distance over which the prayer may be shortened, because His words "when you travel through the land" mean travel in general. For this reason, the Zahiris permitted shortening in every journey, whether long or short. The position of Malik and al-Shafi'i is that the required distance is forty-eight miles, and they relied on reports from 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas. Likewise, the verse does not indicate that shortening is restricted to a journey of obedience or a permissible journey, excluding a journey of sin, since its wording is unrestricted regarding travel. For this reason, Abu Hanifa permitted shortening in a journey of obedience, in a permissible journey, and in a journey of sin. Malik prohibited it in a journey of sin, and Ibn Hanbal prohibited it in both a journey of sin and a permissible journey. Shortening has rulings that are not connected to the verse, so we have set aside mention of them. The meaning of "fitnah" (trial, temptation) in this verse is fighting or attack that is disliked.

The commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verses 102-103:

﴿And when you are among them﴾ The verse concerns the prayer of fear (ṣalāt al-khawf, the prayer performed in a state of danger). Its apparent meaning implies that it is not to be performed after the Messenger of God (ﷺ) has passed away, since the condition set is his presence among them. Abu Yusuf held this view. The majority (al-jumhur) permitted it after his death (ﷺ), because they understood that the address to him includes his community. The Companions performed it after him (ﷺ). The scholars differed over the prayer of fear in ten opinions, due to the differing reports about it. We need not mention them, since its interpretation does not depend on them. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) performed the prayer of fear during the Battle of Dhat al-Riqa'.

﴿So let a party of them stand with you﴾ The imam divides the Muslims into two groups. He leads the first group in half the prayer, while the other group stands guarding. Then he leads the second group in the remainder of the prayer, while the first group stands guarding. The scholars differed over whether each group completes its prayer; this is the view of the majority, though some disagree. On the view that they complete it, they differed over whether they complete it immediately after their prayer with the imam or afterward.

﴿And let them take their weapons﴾ The scholars differed over who is commanded to take up weapons. It was said to be the group that prays, and it was said to be the group that guards. The first view is preferred, because He later said of the other group: ﴿And let them take their precaution and their weapons﴾. This indicates that if they are attacked while in prayer, it is permissible for them to fight those who attack them. Otherwise, taking up weapons would have no purpose if they did not use them to repel those who attack them.

﴿Then when they have prostrated, let them be behind you﴾ The pronoun in "when they have prostrated" refers to the praying group. The meaning is: when they have prostrated with you in the first rak'ah. It was also said: when they have prostrated in the rak'ah of making up the prayer. The pronoun in "let them be behind you" may refer to those who prostrated, meaning: when they have prostrated, let them rise and go behind you. On this reading, if the prostration was in the first rak'ah, it implies that they rise to guard after the first rak'ah has ended. Then they may complete the rest of their prayer or not complete it. If the prostration was in the rak'ah of making up the prayer, it implies that they do not rise to guard until after completing it. This is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. The pronoun in "let them be behind you" may also refer to the other group, meaning that they stand behind the praying ones to guard them.

﴿And let another party come forward﴾ This means the guarding group.

﴿Those who disbelieve wish that you would neglect your weapons and your baggage, so they could attack you in one swoop﴾ This verse reports what took place during the Battle of Dhat al-Riqa', namely the disbelievers' determination to strike the Muslims when they were occupied with their prayer. Gabriel came down to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of this. The prayer of fear was legislated as a precaution against the disbelievers. In His words "in one swoop", there is emphasis: it means a single attack, without the need for a second.

﴿There is no blame upon you if you put down your arms because of rain or if you are ill﴾ This verse was revealed concerning Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf. He was ill and set down his weapon, and some people rebuked him. So God granted permission to put down weapons in the case of illness and rain. Any other excuse that arises at that time is analogous to these two.

﴿Indeed, God has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾ If it is asked: how does the command to take precaution correspond to the humiliating punishment? The answer is that the command to be cautious of the enemy implies a fear of their strength and might. So He negated that fear by informing that God humiliates them and does not grant them victory, in order to strengthen the hearts of the believers. Al-Zamakhshari said this. However, this is valid only if the humiliating punishment is in this world, while the more apparent meaning is that it is in the Hereafter.

﴿So when you have completed your rites [of pilgrimage], remember God﴾ [al-Baqara: 200]. This means: when you have finished the prayer, remember God with your tongues. The mention of standing, sitting, and lying on the sides is to encompass all states of a person. It was also said that the meaning is: when you are engaged in prayer, perform it standing; if you cannot, then sitting; if you cannot, then on your sides.

﴿So when you are secure, establish the prayer﴾ That is, when you are free from fear, establish the prayer in its known form.

﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at fixed times [kitaban mawquta]﴾ That is, limited to fixed times. Ibn Abbas said: it means obligatory.

It was also said that the meaning is: when you are engaged in prayer, perform it standing; if you cannot, then sitting; if you cannot, then on your sides.

﴿So when you are secure, establish the prayer﴾ That is, when you are free from fear, establish the prayer in its known form.

﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at fixed times [kitaban mawquta]﴾ That is, limited to fixed times. Ibn Abbas said: it means obligatory.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 104:

﴿And do not lose heart in pursuing the enemy﴾: that is, do not weaken in seeking out the disbelievers. ﴿If you are suffering pain, then indeed they are suffering pain as you are suffering﴾: its meaning is: if pain from fighting afflicts you, then likewise pain similar to it afflicts the disbelievers. Moreover, you hope, when you fight them, for victory in this world and reward in the Hereafter; and that is an encouragement to the Muslims.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 105–106:

﴿That you may judge between the people by what Allah has shown you﴾ It may be that he means by revelation, or by ijtihad (independent reasoning), or by both. If it includes ijtihad, then in it is evidence for the validity of reasoning (nazar) and analogy (qiyas), contrary to those who prohibit this, such as the Zahiriyya (the literalist school) and others. ﴿And do not be a pleader for the treacherous﴾ This verse and what follows were revealed concerning the story of Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq, when he stole food and a weapon belonging to one of the Ansar. His people came to the Prophet ﷺ and said that he was innocent, and they attributed the theft to someone else. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ thought they were truthful, so he argued on their behalf to ward off what had been attributed to them, until the Qur'an was revealed and they were exposed. So the "treacherous" in the verse are the thieves, the sons of Ubayriq. Al-Suhayli said: they were Bishr, Bashir, Mubashshir and Usayd. Its meaning is: do not be a disputant for the sake of the treacherous against others. ﴿And seek forgiveness from Allah﴾ That is, for your pleading on behalf of the treacherous. This is so because he ﷺ spoke according to the outward appearance, while he believed in their innocence.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verses 108–113:

﴿When they plot by night, saying what He does not approve.﴾ That is, they devise (yudabbirūn) at night. The planning is called "saying" (qawl) because it is speech of the soul (kalam al-nafs), though it may be accompanied by speech of the tongue.

﴿And whoever earns a sin﴾ It has been said: a khaṭī'ah (error or wrongdoing) may occur intentionally or unintentionally, whereas ithm (sin) occurs only intentionally. It has also been said: the two have the same meaning, and the term is repeated because the wording differs.

﴿Then throws it upon an innocent person﴾ The people had attributed the theft to Labid ibn Sahl.

﴿A group of them had resolved to lead you astray﴾ They are the ones who came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and declared Ibn Abi al-Abirq innocent of the theft. Although this verse was revealed because of this incident, it also contains rulings applicable to other cases. The remainder of the verse is an honor to the Prophet (ﷺ) and an enumeration of the blessings of Allah upon him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verses 114–115:

﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk﴾. If al-najwa (secret talk) here means hidden speech, then the exception that follows it is disjunctive (munqati'). It may also be connective (muttasil) by omitting a noun (mudaf): the sense is "except the secret talk of one who enjoins...". If al-najwa means a group (jama'ah), then the exception is connective.

﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger﴾, i.e., shows enmity to him. Al-shiqaq (opposition) is enmity. The verse was revealed concerning Ibn al-Abyraq, for he apostatized, joined the polytheists, and died in disbelief. It is general in application to him and to others.

﴿And follows other than the way of the believers﴾. The usulis (jurists of legal theory) have used this to establish that the consensus (ijma') of the Muslims is valid and that it is not permissible to oppose it, because whoever opposes it follows other than the way of the believers. Yet there is room for scrutiny in this.

﴿We shall leave him to what he has turned to﴾, i.e., we shall leave him with his corrupt choice.

Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 4, verses 116–117:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ The discussion of its counterpart has already been presented. ﴿They invoke, instead of Him, none but females﴾. The pronoun in "yad'una" (they invoke) refers to the disbelievers, and the meaning of "yad'una" is "ya'budun" (they worship). The scholars differed regarding "al-inath" (females) here. He said "they worship him" because they obey him in disbelief and misguidance. "Marid" (rebellious) is one who is extremely defiant and misleading.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verses 118–121:

﴿Allah cursed him﴾: an attribute of Satan. ﴿And he said, "I will surely take from among Your servants an appointed portion"﴾: the pronoun refers to Satan, meaning: I have appropriated it for myself, from your saying "fard lil-jund" (he assigned a share/stipend to the soldiers) and others. By "them" is meant the people of misguidance. ﴿And I will surely mislead them﴾, i.e., I will give them false hopes (al-amani al-kadhiba). ﴿And they will surely slit the ears of cattle﴾, i.e., they will cut them, and the reference by "that" is to the bahira and the like. ﴿And they will surely alter the creation of Allah﴾. The alteration (al-taghyir) is castration and the like. A group of scholars permitted the castration of animals when it is beneficial, while some prohibited it, based on the apparent meaning of the verse. It is also said that the alteration is tattooing and the like, and this is indicated by the hadith in which he cursed the women who tattoo and those who have themselves tattooed, those who pluck their facial hair (al-mutanammisat), those who file their teeth for beauty (al-mutafalijat lil-husn), and those who alter the creation of Allah. ﴿A place of escape﴾, i.e., a means of deviation (mu'addal) and a refuge (mahrab).

The Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 4, verses 122–124:

﴿The promise of Allah, a true promise﴾. Two verbal nouns (maṣdar, pl. maṣādir, a verbal noun). The first emphasizes the promise implied by His saying: "We will admit them into gardens." The second emphasizes Allah's promise. ﴿Not by your wishful thinking﴾ and the verse continues. The ism of laysa (the subject of laysa) is a pronoun whose implied meaning is "the matter" and similar. The address is to the Muslims. It is also said that it is to the polytheists, meaning: what you wish for will not happen, nor will what the People of the Book wish for, but Allah judges among His servants and recompenses them for their deeds. ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ is a definite threat for the disbelievers, and it is conditioned by Allah's will for the Muslims. ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds﴾: min is used for partitive (tab'īd) out of mercy for the servants, because perfect righteous deeds are beyond the capacity of humans. ﴿while being a believer﴾ is a condition requiring faith, for no deed is accepted except with it. ﴿a speck (naqīr)﴾ is the small pit on the back of a date stone, and the meaning is an illustration by the smallest of things.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 125:

﴿And follows the religion of Ibrahim﴾ i.e., the religion of Islam. ﴿Hanif﴾ is a circumstantial state (hal) either of the one who follows or of Ibrahim.

﴿And Allah took Ibrahim as a khalil (intimate friend)﴾ i.e., a ṣafī (chosen one, pure friend). It is derived from al-khulla (khilla), meaning affection and love. In this there is an honouring of Ibrahim and an encouragement to follow him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 127:

﴿They ask you for a legal ruling concerning women﴾ That is, they ask you about what is obligatory for them regarding the matter of women. ﴿And what is recited to you﴾ is a conjunction with the name of Allah, meaning: Allah gives you a ruling. What is recited to you in the Book, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿concerning the orphan women, to whom you do not give what has been prescribed for them﴾. A man among the Arabs would marry an orphan girl from among his relatives without giving her the bridal gift (ṣadāq) that she deserved. So His saying "what has been prescribed for them" means the bridal gift that the woman is entitled to. And His saying ﴿and you desire to marry them﴾ means: for their beauty and their wealth, without fulfilling their rights. So Allah, mighty and majestic, forbade them from that at the beginning of the surah in His saying: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans﴾ [An-Nisa: 3], and so on. This is what was recited to them concerning orphan women. ﴿And the oppressed among the children﴾ is a conjunction with "orphan women." What was recited concerning the oppressed among the children is His saying: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children﴾ [An-Nisa: 11], because the Arabs did not give inheritance to a daughter or to a young son. So Allah commanded that they take their share of the inheritance. ﴿And that you stand firm for the orphans in justice﴾ is a conjunction with "the oppressed." That is, what is recited to you is that you should stand firm for the orphans in justice. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative, its implied meaning being: "and He commands you that you stand firm..." Or the address in this is to the guardians, the trustees (awṣiyā'), or the judges and their like. What was recited to them in this regard is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the properties of orphans unjustly﴾ [An-Nisa: 10], and so on, and His saying: ﴿And do not consume your properties among yourselves unjustly﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 188], and other such verses.

And if a woman fears ill-treatment (nushūz) or aversion from her husband, there is no blame on them if they make a settlement between themselves. The meaning of the verse is the permissibility of settlement between spouses when the wife fears nushūz (marital discord, here meaning the husband's ill-treatment of her) or iʿrāḍ (aversion). Just as settlement is permitted in anticipation of such fear, it is also permitted after nushūz or iʿrāḍ has occurred. The meaning of nushūz has already been explained. As for iʿrāḍ, it is milder. The ways of settlement are many. Among them, the husband gives her something, or she gives him something, or she waives her right to maintenance or to intimacy, or to something else.

The occasion of the revelation was that Sawda bint Zamʿa, when she grew old, feared that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would divorce her. So she said to him: "Keep me among your wives, and do not allot me a night, and I have given my night to ʿĀʾisha." ﴿And settlement is better﴾: this is a general expression that includes settlement between spouses and other settlements. It was also said that its meaning is: settlement between spouses is better than their separation. On this reading, "better" (khayr) is comparative. The definite article in "al-ṣulḥ" (the settlement) is for a known reference (al-ʿahd). ﴿And souls have been made present to stinginess﴾: the meaning is that stinginess (shuḥḥ) has been made present with souls, never absent from them, because they were created disposed to it. Shuḥḥ is that a person does not allow another any of the shares of his own self. The stinginess of the woman in this sense is her demand for her right to maintenance and intimacy. The stinginess of the husband is withholding the dowry, restricting maintenance, and disinclination toward the wife because of her advanced age or her ugliness.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verses 129–130:

﴿And you will never be able to be just between wives﴾ means complete and perfect justice in words, deeds, love and everything else. So God lifted this from His servants, for they are unable to do it. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to divide his time equally among his wives and then say: "O God, this is my division in what I control, so do not hold me accountable for what I do not control," meaning the inclination of the heart. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 135:

﴿Be persistent in upholding justice﴾ — i.e., striving diligently to establish justice. ﴿Witnesses for God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18] — its meaning is for the sake of God's countenance and His good pleasure. ﴿Even if it be against yourselves﴾ — this phrase is connected to "witnesses." A person's testimony against himself is his acknowledgment of the truth. Then he mentioned parents and close relatives, since they are the likely objects of partisanship and inclination. So establishing testimony against strangers is all the more fitting and proper. ﴿Whether he is rich or poor﴾ — the answer to "whether" (in) is omitted, most evidently; i.e., if the one testified against is rich, do not refrain from testifying against him out of deference to him; and if he is poor, do not refrain from testifying against him out of pity, for God is more deserving of (concern for) the rich and the poor, i.e., in regard to them. ﴿So do not follow your desires lest you deviate﴾ — "lest" (an an) is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). It may also be that the meaning is "from justice," so the estimate becomes "in desire that you be just among people," or "from justice," so the estimate becomes "out of aversion that you deviate from the truth." ﴿And if you distort or refuse﴾ — it has been said that the address is to the rulers, and it has been said to the witnesses; the wording is general to both aspects. "Layy" is the distortion of speech, i.e., you distort (your speech) away from judging with justice or away from testifying to the truth, or you turn away from the rightful claimant, or from the one in whose favor the truth is testified. Indeed, God will requite you, for He is well-acquainted with what you do. It is also recited as ﴿taluw﴾ with the lam vowelled with a damma, from wilaya (taking charge): i.e., if you take charge of establishing testimony, or turn away from it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verses 136–137:

﴿Believe in Allah﴾ The verse is an address to the Muslims. Its meaning is a command that their faith be complete in respect of everything mentioned, or it is a command to persist in faith. It was also said: it is an address to the People of the Book who believed in the earlier prophets; its meaning is a command that they also believe in Muhammad ﷺ. It was also said: it is an address to the hypocrites, its meaning being a command that they believe with their tongues and their hearts. ﴿Indeed, those who believed and then disbelieved﴾ (the verse). It was said: it refers to the hypocrites, because of their wavering between faith and disbelief. It was also said: it refers to the Jews and Christians, because they believed in their prophets and then disbelieved in Muhammad ﷺ. The first view is more preferred, because the discussion from this point onward concerns them, and the most apparent view is that it refers to one who believed in Muhammad ﷺ, then apostatized, then returned to faith, then apostatized again and increased in disbelief. ﴿Allah would not be one to forgive them﴾ That applies to one whom Allah knows will die upon his disbelief. Their being led astray may also be a punishment for them due to the evil of their deeds.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verses 148–149:

﴿Except one who has been wronged﴾. That is, the wronged person may raise his voice (al-jahr). It is permissible for him, by way of raising the voice, to invoke curses upon the one who wronged him. It is also said: that he may mention the wrong that was done to him. And it is said: that he may retaliate against him with the like of his wrong, if the other person insulted him. ﴿Whether you disclose a good deed or conceal it﴾ (the verse). This is an exhortation to doing good, both secretly and openly, and to pardoning wrongdoing, after having permitted retaliation (al-intisar). This is because pardon is more beloved to God than retaliation. He emphasized this by describing Himself, exalted is He, as the Pardoner (al-'Afw) while having the power (to punish).

Verse 150 of Surah al-Nisa'

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ etc. It refers to the Jews and the Christians, because they believed in their prophets and disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ) and others. The meaning of "making distinction between Allah and His messengers" is to believe in Him and disbelieve in His messengers. Likewise, making distinction between the messengers is disbelieving in some of them and believing in others. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verses 152–153:

﴿وَٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ﴾ [And those who believe] – the verse: It refers to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), because they believed in Allah and all His messengers. ﴿يَسْأَلُكَ أَهْلُ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ﴾ [The People of the Book ask you] – the verse. It is reported that the Jews said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We will not believe in you until you bring us a book from the heaven all at once, as Moses brought the Torah." It was also said: "A book to so-and-so, and a book to so-and-so, stating that you are the Messenger of Allah." They only asked for this out of obstinacy. Allah mentioned their question to Moses and their bad manners toward him, as consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), so that he might take comfort in following the example of others. Then He mentioned their ugly deeds to show that their disbelief is nothing but stubborn defiance. The mention of their request to see Allah openly, their taking the calf (as a god), the lifting of the Mount (Tur) above them, their transgression concerning the Sabbath, and other things that are alluded to here, has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah.
