Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 157–158:

﴿And for their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary"﴾ Allah counted among their abominations their saying: "Indeed, we killed the Messiah," because they said it boastfully and audaciously, while they were lying in that, and the sin fell upon them. They did not kill him, for they crucified the person upon whom his likeness was cast, and they believed him to be Jesus. It is narrated that Jesus said to the disciples (al-Hawariyyun): "Which of you will have my likeness cast upon him, so that he is killed and becomes my companion in Paradise?" One of them said: "I will," and his likeness was cast upon him, and he was killed thinking he was Jesus. It was also said: rather, a Jew pointed out Jesus, so Allah cast the likeness of Jesus upon the Jew, and the Jew was killed, while Jesus was raised to heaven alive, until he descends to the earth and kills the Dajjal (the Antichrist). ﴿The Messenger of Allah﴾. If it is asked: how did they say of him "the Messenger of Allah," when they disbelieve in him and revile him? The answer has three aspects. First: they said that in the manner of mockery and derision. Second: they said it according to the belief of the Muslims concerning him, as if they said, "the Messenger of Allah, according to you, or by your claim." Third: it is from the speech of Allah, not from their speech, so it is halted before it. The benefit is to magnify their sin and to disparage their saying: "Indeed, we killed him." ﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him﴾ is a refutation of that and a denial of them and of the Christians also in their saying that he was crucified, so that they worshipped the cross on account of that. And the utmost wonder is their contradiction in saying that he is a god or the son of a god, and then saying that he was crucified. ﴿But it was made to appear so to them﴾. In it there are two interpretations. First: what we have mentioned, namely the casting of his likeness upon the disciple or upon the Jew. Second: that its meaning is that the matter was made to appear to them as such; i.e., the people who sought to kill him confused them, so that they killed another man and crucified him, and prevented the people from approaching him until he was disfigured so that he could not be recognized, and they said to the people: "This is Jesus," and it was not Jesus. So the people believed their truthfulness, while they were deliberately lying. ﴿And indeed, those who differed concerning it are in doubt about it﴾. It is narrated that when Jesus was raised and his likeness was cast upon another and they killed him, they said: "If this one killed is Jesus, where is our companion? And if this is our companion, where is Jesus?" So they differed; some of them said, "He is he," and some said, "He is not he." They agreed that a person was killed, but differed as to who he was. ﴿except the following of assumption﴾. This is an exceptive clause that is disconnected (istithna' munqati'), because knowledge is certainty and assumption is hesitation. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is connected, since assumption and knowledge are both included under the genus of beliefs. If it is asked: how did He describe them as in doubt, which is hesitation between two equal possibilities, and then describe them as in assumption, which is preference for one of the two possibilities? The answer is that they were in doubt, then signs appeared to them and they assumed; this was said by al-Zamakhshari. It may also be said: assumption can mean doubt and can mean suspicion (wahm), which is weaker than doubt. ﴿And they did not kill him with certainty﴾. That is, they did not kill him with a certain killing. So the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of yaqinan on this view is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar). It was also said: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state, i.e., they did not kill him while certain. It was also said: it is an emphasis of the negation in His saying "they did not kill him," i.e., they were certain of the negation of his killing, and on this view it is accusative as a verbal noun. ﴿Rather, Allah raised him to Himself﴾. That is, to His heaven. It has been reported in the hadith of the Isra' (Night Journey) that he is in the second heaven.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 157–158:

﴿And for their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary"﴾ Allah counted among their abominations their saying: "Indeed, we killed the Messiah," because they said it boastfully and audaciously, while they were lying in that, and the sin fell upon them. They did not kill him, for they crucified the person upon whom his likeness was cast, and they believed him to be Jesus. It is narrated that Jesus said to the disciples (al-Hawariyyun): "Which of you will have my likeness cast upon him, so that he is killed and becomes my companion in Paradise?" One of them said: "I will," and his likeness was cast upon him, and he was killed thinking he was Jesus. It was also said: rather, a Jew pointed out Jesus, so Allah cast the likeness of Jesus upon the Jew, and the Jew was killed, while Jesus was raised to heaven alive, until he descends to the earth and kills the Dajjal (the Antichrist). ﴿The Messenger of Allah﴾. If it is asked: how did they say of him "the Messenger of Allah," when they disbelieve in him and revile him? The answer has three aspects. First: they said that in the manner of mockery and derision. Second: they said it according to the belief of the Muslims concerning him, as if they said, "the Messenger of Allah, according to you, or by your claim." Third: it is from the speech of Allah, not from their speech, so it is halted before it. The benefit is to magnify their sin and to disparage their saying: "Indeed, we killed him." ﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him﴾ is a refutation of that and a denial of them and of the Christians also in their saying that he was crucified, so that they worshipped the cross on account of that. And the utmost wonder is their contradiction in saying that he is a god or the son of a god, and then saying that he was crucified. ﴿But it was made to appear so to them﴾. In it there are two interpretations. First: what we have mentioned, namely the casting of his likeness upon the disciple or upon the Jew. Second: that its meaning is that the matter was made to appear to them as such; i.e., the people who sought to kill him confused them, so that they killed another man and crucified him, and prevented the people from approaching him until he was disfigured so that he could not be recognized, and they said to the people: "This is Jesus," and it was not Jesus. So the people believed their truthfulness, while they were deliberately lying. ﴿And indeed, those who differed concerning it are in doubt about it﴾. It is narrated that when Jesus was raised and his likeness was cast upon another and they killed him, they said: "If this one killed is Jesus, where is our companion? And if this is our companion, where is Jesus?" So they differed; some of them said, "He is he," and some said, "He is not he." They agreed that a person was killed, but differed as to who he was. ﴿except the following of assumption﴾. This is an exceptive clause that is disconnected (istithna' munqati'), because knowledge is certainty and assumption is hesitation. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is connected, since assumption and knowledge are both included under the genus of beliefs. If it is asked: how did He describe them as in doubt, which is hesitation between two equal possibilities, and then describe them as in assumption, which is preference for one of the two possibilities? The answer is that they were in doubt, then signs appeared to them and they assumed; this was said by al-Zamakhshari. It may also be said: assumption can mean doubt and can mean suspicion (wahm), which is weaker than doubt. ﴿And they did not kill him with certainty﴾. That is, they did not kill him with a certain killing. So the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of yaqinan on this view is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar). It was also said: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state, i.e., they did not kill him while certain. It was also said: it is an emphasis of the negation in His saying "they did not kill him," i.e., they were certain of the negation of his killing, and on this view it is accusative as a verbal noun. ﴿Rather, Allah raised him to Himself﴾. That is, to His heaven. It has been reported in the hadith of the Isra' (Night Journey) that he is in the second heaven.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 159:

﴿And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in him before his death﴾. In it there are two interpretations. The first: the pronoun in "his death" refers to Jesus. The meaning is that every one of the People of the Scripture will believe in Jesus when he descends to the earth, before Jesus dies, and then all the religions will become one religion, which is the religion of Islam. The second: the pronoun in "his death" refers to the Scripture implied by His words, "And there is none of the People of the Scripture," the estimated meaning being: "And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will believe in Jesus and know that he is a prophet before this person dies," and that is at the moment of facing death, and it is a faith that will not benefit him. This meaning has been related from Ibn ʿAbbas and others. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb it reads "before their death," and this reading strengthens the second opinion. The pronoun in "in him" refers to Jesus according to both views. It has also been said that it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 160–164:

﴿And because of their turning away from the way of God, many [people]﴾ may be understood as meaning aversion (i'rad), in which case "kathiran" (many) is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, the implied sense being "a great turning away." Or it may mean their barring others, in which case "kathiran" is the object of the verb of barring: they barred many of the people from the way of God.

﴿But those firm in knowledge among them﴾ are ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, Mukhayriq, and those who were like them.

﴿And those who establish the prayer﴾ is in the accusative case (manṣūb) by way of praise (madḥ), with a verb implied; this is frequent in speech. ʿĀʾisha said it is one of the errors of the scribes of the codex (laḥn kitāb al-muṣḥaf). In the codex of Ibn Masʿud it reads "wa-l-muqīmūn" (in the nominative), which is the original form.

﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you﴾ (the verse): a reply to the Jews who asked the Prophet ﷺ to send down to them a book from the heavens, and an argument against them that what he brought is revelation, just as those prophets before him brought revelation without a book being sent down from the heavens. For this reason he mentioned at length the prophets whose situation was this, so that the proof would be established through them.

﴿And messengers We have related to you before﴾ is in the accusative by a hidden verb, meaning "We sent messengers."

﴿And God spoke to Moses with direct speech﴾ is an explicit statement of speech, emphasized by the verbal noun (taʾkid bi-l-maṣdar). This is evidence against the claim of the Muʿtazila that it was the tree that spoke to Moses.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verses 165–166:

﴿Messengers as bringers of good news﴾ is in the accusative, either governed by a verb implied or as an apposition (badal). ﴿So that people will have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾: that is, Allah sent them to cut off the argument of one who says, "If He had sent a messenger to me, I would have believed." ﴿But Allah bears witness﴾ and the rest of the verse: its meaning is that Allah bears witness that the Qur'an is from Him, and the angels likewise bear witness to that. The occasion of the verse was the denial of revelation by the Jews, so the statement of contrast (istidrak) came on the assumption that they had said, "We will not bear witness to what has been sent down to you," and it was said, "But Allah bears witness to that." Among the rhetorical devices (adawat al-bayan) in the verse is al-tardid (repetition), which is mentioning the witnessing first and then mentioning it again at the end of the verse. ﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾: in this is evidence for the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) for establishing the knowledge of Allah, in contrast to the Mu'tazilah in their claim that He is knowing without knowledge. They have interpreted the verse with a distant interpretation.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verses 170–171:

﴿O mankind﴾: a general address, because the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent to all of humanity. ﴿So believe; it is better for you﴾: here "khayran" is in the accusative as a predicate (khabar), and in His words ﴿Desist; it is better for you﴾ it is governed by a suppressed verb that does not appear, whose estimated form is "ituu khayran lakum" (bring about what is better for you). This is the view of Sibawayh. Al-Khalil said: it is in the accusative by the meaning of "believe" and "desist." Al-Farra' said: "fa-aminu" means "fa-aminu iman khayran lakum," so it is in the accusative as an adjective (na't) of a deleted verbal noun (masdar). The Kufans said: it is the predicate of a deleted "kana" (was), whose estimated form is "yakun al-iman khayran lakum" (let faith be better for you). ﴿And if you disbelieve, then indeed to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾: that is, He is free of need of you, and your disbelief does not harm Him. ﴿O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion﴾: this is an address to the Christians, because they went to extremes regarding Jesus until they disbelieved. So the phrase "People of the Scripture" is a general expression intended in a specific sense, referring to the Christians, as indicated by what follows. "Ghuluw" (extremism) is excessiveness and going beyond the limit. ﴿And His word﴾: that is, a being brought into existence by His word, "Be," without an intermediary of a father or a drop of semen. ﴿And a spirit from Him﴾: that is, one possessing a spirit from Allah. Here "min" indicates the starting point, and the meaning is "from the presence of Allah." He attributed it to Allah because Allah sent Gabriel (peace be upon him) with it to Mary. ﴿And do not say: "Three"﴾: a prohibition against Trinitarianism, which is the doctrine of the Christians. "Thalatha" (three) is the predicate of a suppressed subject (mubtada' mudmar). ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾: this is proof of His exaltation above having a son, because He is the owner of everything.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary on Surah 4, verses 172–175:

﴿Lan yastankifa﴾: "will not disdain," likewise; its meaning is wherever it occurs. ﴿wa-lā al-malā'ikatu﴾: In this there is evidence for those who say that the angels are superior to the prophets, because the meaning is that Jesus will not disdain, nor will those above him [i.e., the angels]. ﴿qad jā'akum burhānun﴾: this is the Qur'an, and it is also the clear light (al-nūr al-mubīn). It is possible that by the proof (al-burhān) he means the evidences and arguments, and by the light he means the Prophet (ﷺ), because God called him a lamp (sirāj).

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 4, verse 176:

﴿They ask you for a ruling﴾: i.e., they ask you to give them a legal opinion (fatwa). It is possible that this verb is the one that governs "al-kalala" (the one who leaves neither ascendants nor descendants), and that "yuftikum" (He gives you a ruling) is also a request for it; in that case it falls under the category of *i'mal* (the grammatical principle of two verbs governing one noun), with the second verb being the operative one according to the school of the Basrans. Alternatively, "yastaftunaka" may be cut off from what follows and a pause made upon it. The first reading is more apparent. The meaning of *al-kalala* has already been explained at the beginning of the surah. What is meant here by "the sister and the brother" is the full (shaqa'iq) siblings, and the paternal siblings when there are no full siblings. The ruling on maternal siblings has already been mentioned in His words: ﴿And if a man leaves neither ascendants nor descendants, but has a brother or a sister...﴾. ﴿If a man dies﴾: the word "imru'" is in the nominative case by a verb understood, according to the Basrans. There is no difficulty in what is mentioned here concerning the laws of inheritance. ﴿Lest you go astray﴾: this is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), its implied sense being "out of dislike that you should go astray."
